Gifting, Resale and the Power of Experiences: The Watch Industry Is in Its Customer Service Era

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2731 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A mixture of high-level customer service, personal experiences, and frictionless shopping has helped watchmakers improve their image and perceived value among consumers this year.
  • It has been revealed that watch brands’ awareness among consumers is on the rise, and this moves in lockstep with overall positive associations.
  • Despite pressure from higher gold prices and a strong Swiss franc that has forced watchmakers to raise prices across the board in recent years, respondents still consider watches a good investment, increasingly purchase them as gifts, and remain loyal to their brands of choice even when confronted with price rises.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A mixture of high-level customer service, personal experiences, and frictionless shopping has helped watchmakers improve their image and perceived value among consumers this year.

It has been revealed that watch brands’ awareness among consumers is on the rise, and this moves in lockstep with overall positive associations. In this scenario, established brands have strengthened their position, while smaller brands have found fertile ground to grow.

Despite pressure from higher gold prices and a strong Swiss franc that has forced watchmakers to raise prices across the board in recent years, respondents still consider watches a good investment, increasingly purchase them as gifts, and remain loyal to their brands of choice even when confronted with price rises.

The recent excitement around resale schemes, limited editions, in-person services, immediate stock availability and exhibitions spotlights an appetite for proximity, access and the human touch, offering opportunities for brands that can support customers across multiple touchpoints and build communities.

Industry observers note that at the top of the innovation table, the best performers — Rolex, Cartier, Omega, Patek Philippe, and Tag Heuer — each maintained their position in the 2026 Vogue Business Watch Index, even improving their score. Rolex keeps its crown for overall consumer sentiment, achieving 99% aided awareness, and Tag Heuer boosts its aided awareness score by 2 percentage points. Despite Breitling, in sixth position, improving its overall brand awareness ranking from 72% to 73%, driven by improvements in aided awareness, the gap with Tag Heuer for overall awareness widened to 8 percentage points.

The most striking result of the Index is that 75% of the brands surveyed have seen their awareness score improve, bringing the overall average awareness score up by 1.6 percentage points, which means the public is more aware of the watch category as a whole and readily recognizes brands.

In a recent development, chopard takes the crown as the top performer by improving its awareness score by 6 percentage points from 62% last year to 68% this year. It is followed by Longines, A. Lange & Söhne, and Vacheron Constantin, which improved by 4 percentage points, and Piaget, Audemars Piguet, IWC, and Movado, which improved their score by 3 percentage points.

Interestingly, this year the top five brands improved their overall awareness (combined aided and unaided awareness) score by 1 percentage point to an average of 90%, while the other 15 surveyed brands registered a higher increase of 1.8 percentage points. This means the challengers are putting more pressure on the top five, but with an average aggregated awareness of 58.4%, the gap is still wide.

The awareness ranking is particularly relevant because it demonstrates a strong correlation with brand equity, consumer sentiment, and purchase intent, particularly for the top five performers.

Recent findings suggest that but awareness alone does not translate into purchase intent across the board, as purchase intent far lags awareness. Rolex, the top performer, ranked first across all criteria, has only 38% purchase intent, but in a ranking methodology, becomes the “100%” player to which all other brands are indexed. Across the board, purchase intent is relatively flat vs. last year, with actual purchase intent sitting at 16% on average across all brands. This means that brands with relatively modest purchase intent, such as A. Lange & Söhne at 14%, perform above average when ranked (coming in at 58% in the ranking), given the economic pressures on purchase intent. Yet this methodology does expose just how competitive the landscape is. When we rank purchase intent, A. Lange & Söhne is comparable to IWC, despite the latter enjoying significantly higher brand awareness, with aided awareness sitting 25 percentage points higher. In contrast, brands such as Breitling, Hublot and Tudor display high awareness ranking scores (Breitling 73%, Hublot 66%, and Tudor 49%) but actual purchase intent of just 12% and 13%.

Interestingly, brand loyalty has increased to 64.3% vs 63% last year, as consumers resist the temptation to switch to a more affordable brand even if prices increase, with the 45-64 age group having the strongest resolve. Nevertheless, that same demographic demonstrates a higher propensity to explore discounts and resale options, still showing some price sensitivity.

In 2025, Vogue Business asked luxury watch consumers about their watch-buying habits for gifting occasions in the Middle East. This year, we extended that question to all markets. The results reveal interesting motives for buying luxury timepieces, as well as how this varies by local culture.

Sources indicate that overall, key occasions include birthdays (34.1%), Valentine’s Day (29.7%) and Christmas (27.6%), as well as weddings and engagements, particularly for Gen Z (30%) and Gen X (31%). Interestingly, the 40% of luxury consumers who spend more on luxury watches (over $5,000 in the last five years) show a higher propensity to buy luxury watches as gifts for others across every occasion.

Self-gifting has also become a prevalent trend. China is the leading market for personal birthday buys, at 55%, compared with 32% when buying for others. In the Middle East, self-purchasing for birthdays sits at just 32%. Instead, Eid is the leading self-gifting occasion, at 38% — far outpacing buying for others at 24%. This indicates many shoppers are taking advantage of seasonal deals for their own interests. The self-gifting trend also reveals interesting behavior for romantic occasions: a fifth (20%) of luxury consumers in the UK say they have bought themselves luxury watches as an anniversary present in the last two years — double the percentage of French consumers who’ve done the same (10%). Curiously, the opposite is true for weddings and engagements, where only 10% of UK luxury watch consumers shop for this occasion, but 17% of French consumers do. This shows how nuanced gifting occasions are by market, and how the hierarchy of milestones and relationships differs across cultures.

For many years, watch brands have pursued partnerships with the automotive industry, but lately this association seems to be influencing the watchmaking business model, which is increasingly leaning toward the car-making industry’s emphasis on service, a greater focus on experiences and integrated resale options.

When it comes to executing the latter, interestingly, it is the youngest, independent brands such as Richard Mille, MB&F, F.P.Journe and Urwerk that have grasped the importance of owning their secondary market, which leads not only to better control over prices and the products’ retained value but also promotes proximity to clients who, in turn, tend to be more loyal to the brand, act as natural ambassadors, and form communities.

Recent findings suggest that the launch of certified pre-owned schemes has been one of the most significant milestones in the watch industry. While Cartier pioneered the concept in the 1990s, other watch specialists such as Vacheron Constantin and Rolex joined only in the last five years. At the end of October, Audemars Piguet introduced its “Watch Keepers”, its own certified pre-owned program, which will operate as a digital platform enabling sales at a fixed price as well as auctions. It is launching in Europe and Switzerland first before expanding into the United States.

Brand-owned retail platforms allow brands to retain customers who are loyal to the brand but seek more cost-effective options when prices rise. It’s a concern that affects nearly half of all luxury watch consumers, at 47%, with this rising by age as older shoppers say they will shop more for sales and discounts.

Last year’s Vogue Business Watch Index highlighted how brands with low awareness scores were associated with strong purchase intent. This insight is driving brands to purposefully cultivate their niche and strengthen their bond with clients through ad hoc partnerships, without venturing into high-cost, high-visibility collaborations.

Industry observers note that the most interesting success story is that of A. Lange & Söhne because, unlike all other brands surveyed, it is not Swiss but German — and its history, which began in 1845 in Glashütte, stalled between 1945 and 1990, when the brand was relaunched.

In a recent development, from the start, A. Lange & Söhne has cultivated its difference, expanded organically, and gradually grown its base of collectors and buyers with a laser focus on products and selected partnerships. The brand forged strong links early on with prestigious cultural institutions in Dresden, the capital of Saxony, where Glashütte is located. These include the brand’s support for the Dresden State Art Collections (Staatliche Kunstsammlungen Dresden) and the Semperoper opera house, which have run for over 20 years. As part of these tie-ups, the brand supported the exhibition “Paula Modersohn-Becker and Edvard Munch. The Massive Questions of Life” this year. Such partnerships show collectors who visit the brand’s manufacture how the brand is deeply interwoven into the cultural fabric of the area it comes from.

It has been revealed that more recently, A. Lange & Söhne has built on that art legacy by partnering with car events such as the Concours d’Elegance in Hampton Court (UK), Como (Italy) and Newport, Rhode Island (US), known as Audrain Newport Concours & Motor Week. At the end of 2025, the brand opened two new stores, one in London and one in Singapore, while in June this year, it opened its first store in Lisbon.

It has been revealed that other brands following this approach are Jaeger-LeCoultre, with 58% aided awareness, Piaget at 70% awareness, and IWC at 59%. For these brands, criteria such as “its products are a good investment”, “interesting story brand”, and “heritage” seemed to move the needle strongly in consumers’ perceptions.

It has been revealed that these brands have all followed the same restrained and laser-focused blueprint. Boasting an uninterrupted history since its founding in 1833 in Le Sentier, Switzerland, Jaeger-LeCoultre has privileged experiences and exhibitions. At the end of last year, the brand inaugurated its installation “The Dream Shaper” in Shanghai, which showcased over 70 archival pieces and celebrated the brand’s heritage in crafting ladies’ watches. The event was attended by the brand’s ambassadors, including South Korean actor Kim Woo-bin. This year, Jaeger-LeCoultre celebrated its signature Reverso design with a series of dedicated in-store experiences, “Reverso Stories”, as well as some limited-edition pieces presented during Homo Faber in Venice in September.

Piaget has strengthened its commitment to the arts by renewing its partnership with The Andy Warhol Foundation, which led to newly introduced limited-edition pieces this year. The brand also sponsors the Prix Solo Art Genève, a prize awarded to the best solo show during Art Genève. Meanwhile, IWC has cultivated its difference by continuing its association with Formula 1 and highlighting the uniqueness of its heritage with the launch of IWC. Curated — since the end of 2025, some IWC watches from the Maison’s museum have been selected for reproduction and sold in limited quantities.

Sources indicate that cartier staged the second part of its brand exhibition in Melbourne, Australia; Panerai unveiled a showcase in its hometown of Florence, while Patek Philippe brought its retrospective exhibition to Milan. The exhibition, which ran from October 2-18, showcased over 500 pieces and attracted 68,000 visitors. Analysts agree that such exhibitions not only boost the brand equity of the company organizing them, but also increase the general public’s interest in watchmaking.

This year’s most significant trend was the relaunch of milestone designs that ticked most of the boxes that get consumers excited, namely vintage, heritage and limited editions.

One of the most recent examples is Hublot’s Classic Fusion Tributo, which the brand developed with its founder, Carlo Crocco, who also served as the unofficial ambassador for the occasion, marking the first time he has collaborated with Hublot since selling it to LVMH in 2008.

The newly introduced watch, launched in October in Milan this year, is an almost identical reproduction of the model that made Hublot famous in 1980. It features a gold case with screws that also serve as hour indices, mounted on a black rubber strap that, thanks to technological advances, is odorless and does not need to be infused with vanilla like the original 1980s version. The launch allowed clients to meet the brand’s founder and hear directly from him how the watch ended up on the wrist of King Constantine II of Greece, who also gifted one to his brother-in-law, King Juan Carlos of Spain, among other illustrious personalities such as Princess Caroline of Monaco, Elton John and Giorgio Armani.

Hublot’s executive team told the press at the launch that Gen Z’s interest in vintage pieces with a small dial prompted them to launch the project three years early, ahead of the model’s 50th anniversary.

Recent findings suggest that chopard’s relaunch of the original Happy Diamonds watch also marks the celebration of its 50th anniversary. At a party during Fresh York Fashion Week hosted by brand ambassador Bella Hadid, Chopard introduced the new Happy Sport Heritage, reproducing the original cushion-shaped, golden case framing an onyx dial over which diamonds float freely, and mounted on a black leather strap. Chopard also seized the opportunity to relaunch the original Happy Sport designed in 1993 by the creative director and co-president Caroline Scheufele. Happy Sport was conceived as an evolution of the original Happy Diamonds watch and marked the first time diamonds were paired with steel.

CEO, Watches of Switzerland Group.

Industry observers note that in your latest annual report, client experience is mentioned as a growth pillar. What does it mean?

Watches of Switzerland excels in two very different categories: one-time buyers and serial collectors who own hundreds of timepieces. This means we have to offer a variety of services to satisfy the very different demands of these two groups.

Sources indicate that for example, those who only buy one or two watches in their lives may welcome our financing options, as well as the education our salespeople provide to help them buy with confidence something they can treasure and pass on. For dedicated collectors, we focus on providing access to exceptional timepieces and bringing them closer to the brands and the world of watchmaking.

We regularly treat our best clients to manufacturer visits, take them to watch fairs such as Watches and Wonders, and secure exceptional watches. For example, this week, we are inviting them to discover all the timepieces recognized with prestigious GPHG watchmaking awards (Grand Prix d'Horlogerie de Genève), including the independent Rexhep Rexhepi and the gem-set Piaget Sautoir watch.

Sources indicate that watches of Switzerland’s Knightsbridge store. About half of the retailer’s business comes from supply-limited brands such as Rolex and Patek Philippe, and it uses AI to decide what else goes in its windows.

According to recent reports, stock availability is a top priority for clients. What do you do to ensure your stores have the right products?

About half of our business relies on brands such as Rolex and Patek Philippe, which have limited supply and are sold to customers who have waited patiently. But we use artificial intelligence tools to identify trends. For example, when customers browse our watches online, our tool ignores the brand and detects specific watch attributes, such as case size, price point, and strap material; these criteria help us adjust our stock accordingly.

How do you turn digital activity into a commercial opportunity?

According to recent reports, unlike other apparel items, watches can be appreciated even more online, as we can show minute details that are not visible to the naked eye, and we can even show the movement, the beating heart of a timepiece, which is often hidden. We, of course, offer online chats with experts, and one of our points of difference is that we own Hodinkee, the most trusted online watch magazine, with shopping links to our website.

Women are becoming more notable for the watch industry; how are you supporting this growth?

Industry observers note that our new store in Glasgow is a good example: the team there is led by a woman, and the salesforce is evenly split 50-50 between men and women. We also have three watchmakers in residence to service timepieces: one man and two women.

Recent findings suggest that the Vogue Business consumer sentiment ranking assesses brands based on consumers’ opinions and willingness to buy. The criteria analyzed range from basic brand awareness to brand loyalty and purchase intent. Brands are also evaluated on perceived quality, with survey participants answering questions about customer service, in-store experience, design, and sustainability, among others. Respondents have also appraised a brand’s storytelling, role in society, perceived timelessness, digital content, trust, and sense of style.

What Is Smart Aging? Experts Explain the Skin Care Shift Replacing Antiaging

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1566 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elle

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor.
  • Beauty terminology has evolved quite rapidly in recent years—particularly around aging.
  • It has been revealed that natalia Guzman, FNP-C, CANS, a board-certified nurse practitioner at Atelier Aesthetix in Beverly Hills, explains that smart aging is a proactive, science-based approach to maintaining healthy, youthful-looking skin while embracing the natural aging process.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Beauty terminology has evolved quite rapidly in recent years—particularly around aging. What was long labeled antiaging has shifted toward more realistic definitions of what happens to skin and the body as we get older. But the latest buzzword, longevity, as ubiquitous as it’s become, doesn’t exactly fill the gap for those seeking ways to keep skin, hair, and the body looking youthful. Hailey Bieber’s recent use of the term “smart aging” just may be the word substitute the category has been missing.

It has been revealed that natalia Guzman, FNP-C, CANS, a board-certified nurse practitioner at Atelier Aesthetix in Beverly Hills, explains that smart aging is a proactive, science-based approach to maintaining healthy, youthful-looking skin while embracing the natural aging process. “Rather than trying to ‘stop’ aging altogether, which is biologically impossible, smart aging focuses on understanding how our skin changes over time and making informed decisions to preserve a healthy, strong, overall youthful appearance,” Guzman tells ELLE.

It has been revealed that from a dermatologic perspective, Dr. Brianna Olamiju, a board-certified dermatologist with Spring Street Dermatology in NYC, offers this explanation: “Smart aging is about being proactive, making informed skin care choices, and supporting the skin’s natural functions over time. It involves protecting the skin from environmental damage, maintaining a healthy skin barrier, stimulating collagen production when appropriate, and addressing concerns such as fine lines, wrinkles, uneven pigmentation, and loss of elasticity,” says Olamiju. Ultimately, she says, smart aging is about helping your skin look and feel its best at every stage of life while embracing the natural aging process.

Guzman emphasizes that aging beautifully isn’t about looking young. “It’s about looking and feeling like the best version of yourself at every stage of life.”.

As skin evolves, collagen production gradually declines, cellular turnover slows, and environmental factors such as UV exposure, pollution, and lifestyle habits contribute to visible signs of aging. Guzman adds that smart aging means addressing these changes strategically through preventative skin care, healthy lifestyle choices, and, when appropriate, evidence-based aesthetic treatments. “I like to think of smart aging as investing in your skin’s future and being proactive rather than waiting until significant changes occur and attempting to reverse them,” Guzman says. “A lot of the time, the latter takes much more work, and sometimes it cannot be completely corrected.”.

In a recent development, according to Guzman, the biggest difference between smart aging and traditional antiaging is the philosophy behind it. “For decades, the beauty industry has promoted the idea that aging is something we need to fight, prevent, or erase,” notes Guzman. The term “antiaging” often focuses on correcting visible signs of aging, such as wrinkles, volume loss, pigmentation, and skin laxity.

Sources indicate that both Guzman and Olamiju agree that smart aging takes a more holistic, comprehensive, and realistic approach. Olamiju says that anti-aging creates the expectation that we should try to look younger indefinitely. “Smart aging shifts the focus toward skin health, prevention, and maintaining long-term skin quality. Rather than viewing wrinkles, fine lines, and changes in skin textureas something that must be eliminated, smart aging encourages us to support the skin as it naturally evolves. It is less about fighting aging and more about aging well,” she explains. This approach, she adds, also emphasizes consistency, prevention, and individualized treatments rather than chasing every newly introduced product or cosmetic trend.

Guzman adds that smart aging, instead of fighting age, means working with the skin’s biology to help it function and look its best for as long as possible. “The main difference is that we’re not simply chasing wrinkles. We're creating a long-term strategy that prioritizes skin quality, natural-looking results, and overall skin health,” Guzman emphasizes. “To me, anti-aging is often about correcting what we see today, while smart aging is about preventing and protecting what we’ll see tomorrow.”.

It has been revealed that olamiju and Guzman are completely aligned on the first step in a smart aging routine: wearing sunscreen daily. “The foundation of smart aging starts with a consistent skincare routine and healthy lifestyle habits. Daily broad-spectrum sunscreen with an SPF of at least 30 is arguably the most notable step because ultraviolet exposure is one of the leading contributors to premature skin aging, including wrinkles, loss of elasticity, and uneven pigmentation,” states Olamiju. Guzman adds that UV exposure contributes significantly to collagen breakdown and changes in skin texture, noting that sunscreen is essential even on cloudy days.

Olamiju also recommends incorporating topical antioxidants, such as vitamin C, to help protect against environmental oxidative stress, along with moisturizers containing ingredients like ceramides and hyaluronic acid to support hydration and the skin barrier. “Retinoids, including retinol and prescription tretinoin, can be beneficial for improving fine lines, skin texture, and collagen production, provided they are appropriate for the individual,” Olamiju describes.

Paula's Choice Resist Youth-Extending Daily Hydrating Fluid SPF 50.

Dermalogica AGE Smart Biolumin-C Serum.

Sunday Riley Ceramor Ceramide Barrier Replenishing Cream.

SkinMedica Retinol Complex 0.5 Serum.

Bio-Therapeutic bt-sculpt Gen2 Microcurrent Facial Sculpting System.

Once your at-home routine is in place, Guzman recommends strategically incorporating preventive and corrective aesthetic treatments. “Depending on the patient’s age, anatomy, and concerns, treatments such as neuromodulators, collagen-stimulating injectables, microneedling, and energy-based devices may help maintain or improve certain aspects of skin appearance,” says Guzman. The key, she adds, is choosing the right treatment for the right patient rather than following every upcoming aesthetic trend. Olamiju includes chemical peels in a very similar list of in-office treatments, depending, of course, on an individual’s concerns, skin type, and goals.

It has been revealed that finally, the experts agree: don’t underestimate lifestyle. Adequate sleep, regular exercise, balanced nutrition rich in antioxidants and healthy fats, avoiding smoking, managing chronic stress, and limiting excessive alcohol consumption all contribute to overall health and can influence how our skin looks and functions.

Recent findings suggest that the best time to start is earlier than most people think, Olamiju shares. Ideally in your 20s, when prevention can have a meaningful long-term impact. “This does not mean that someone in their 20s needs an elaborate skincare routine or aggressive cosmetic treatments. Rather, it is an opportunity to establish healthy habits, including daily sunscreen use, gentle cleansing, and consistent moisturizing,” notes Olamiju.

Guzman advises starting a smart aging routine before you feel like you need to correct something, but it’s also never too late to begin. “I encourage patients to think of smart aging as something that evolves with them rather than a routine that begins at a specific birthday,” she adds, offering this decade-by-decade breakdown:.

In your 20s. The priority should be prevention. This means establishing healthy skincare habits, wearing sunscreen consistently, maintaining hydration, and introducing targeted active ingredients when appropriate. At this stage, the goal isn’t to aggressively treat aging. It's to protect the skin and build a strong foundation.

According to recent reports, in your 30s. You may begin noticing subtle changes in skin texture, fine lines, pigmentation, or elasticity. This is often a good time to reassess your skin care routine and consider professional treatments based on individual needs. It may also be time to consider a little Botox, energy-based treatments, and biostimulators, all depending on the individual’s needs.

In your 40s and 50s. Changes in collagen, facial volume, skin elasticity, and hormonal influences may become more noticeable. A smart aging approach at this stage may include a combination of medical-grade skin care, collagen-supporting treatments, and continued careful selection of aesthetic procedures.

In your 60s and beyond. The focus remains on maintaining skin health, supporting the skin barrier, addressing concerns such as dryness and uneven pigmentation, and choosing treatments that respect the skin’s changing needs.

Olamiju adds that even patients who begin prioritizing their skin health later in life can benefit significantly from consistent sun protection and an appropriately tailored skin care regimen.

Industry observers note that guzman notes this is one of the most crucial conversations we should be having in modern aesthetics. Both experts say smart aging is not a one-size-fits-all concept. They explain that different skin types and skin tones can experience visible aging differently, and understanding those differences is essential to creating a safe and effective treatment strategy.

It has been revealed that individuals with lighter skin tones may notice fine lines, redness, and visible sun damage earlier, particularly if they have a history of significant UV exposure. Those with darker skin tones may have more visible concerns related to uneven pigmentation, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, and changesin skin tone. “Melanin provides some natural protection against ultraviolet radiation, but it does not eliminate the risk of sun damage or skin cancer, so daily sunscreen remains essential for all skin tones,” Olamiju warns.

According to recent reports, guzman adds that these pigmentation concerns also become especially notable when we introduce aesthetic treatments such as lasers, chemical peels, or microneedling. “Certain procedures and treatment settings carry a greater risk of pigmentation changes in patients with more melanin-rich skin, so proper patient selection, device choice, and clinical expertise are critical,” Guzman notes.

Overall, smart aging should combine science, prevention, consistency, and thoughtful aesthetic care. “Aging is inevitable. How we care for ourselves throughout that process is where we have the opportunity to make a meaningful difference,” Guzman concludes.

K-Pop Stars, Art and Unexpected Collabs: Inside the 2026 Watch Innovation Playbook

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3103 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, after a tough 2025 for the watch industry, 2026 has painted a sunnier picture.
  • Nevertheless, after the shock of the annus horribilis that was 2025, most brands have reviewed their investments, typically ditching high-cost, high-visibility sponsorships in favor of projects that deliver more immediate, tangible results.
  • Following in the footsteps of Rolex, which left Formula 1 sponsorship to LVMH-owned brands, Hublot reduced its involvement in soccer to strengthen collaborations with artists and existing ambassadors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, after a tough 2025 for the watch industry, 2026 has painted a sunnier picture. Overall export value has grown by 2.7% thanks to unexpected pockets of growth in emerging markets (India +28.5%, Thailand +8.6%, and Mexico +6.2%), which offset drops in traditionally strong markets like China (-5.9%) and Saudi Arabia (-10.3%).

Nevertheless, after the shock of the annus horribilis that was 2025, most brands have reviewed their investments, typically ditching high-cost, high-visibility sponsorships in favor of projects that deliver more immediate, tangible results.

Following in the footsteps of Rolex, which left Formula 1 sponsorship to LVMH-owned brands, Hublot reduced its involvement in soccer to strengthen collaborations with artists and existing ambassadors. Ambassadorship became an evolving concept this year, with brands moving beyond campaign appearances to involve their ambassadors in creating the timepieces they promote: Audemars Piguet released a watch co-designed with tennis player Serena Williams, Movado teamed up with American rapper Ludacris, and Hublot unveiled a watch by British designer Samuel Ross. Another defining ambassador trend has been the emergence of partnerships with non-Western talents predominantly from South Korea, Thailand and India, countries that are delivering positive results for the watch business.

Industry observers note that brands have also been experimenting with collaboration projects outside the typical realms of sports and cars. Visual art has emerged as the watchmakers’ latest playground, with Vacheron Constantin unveiling its first mentorship project with The Met in New York and Piaget releasing another watch made in collaboration with The Andy Warhol Foundation. But there were also some unexpected twists, notably with Roger Dubuis teaming up with tattoo artist Dr Woo and Hublot partnering with artist Jeff Koons for timepieces.

Hublot’s partnership with artist Jeff Koons.

Sources indicate that brands also ventured into upcoming partnerships. Richard Mille teamed up with the Italian high-end bicycle manufacturer Colnago, Zenith partnered with furniture maker USM, while Ulysse Nardin established an innovative tie-up with pastry chef Amaury Guichon for its Unstoppable Spirits campaign. This suggests that engagement with the luxury watch category is also operating as a gateway to more niche cultural and lifestyle pursuits.

But collaborations between watch brands were the most prominent modus operandi of 2026. Audemars Piguet and Swatch took center stage with their Royal Pop collection, while Louis Vuitton partnered with independent watchmaker De Bethune and Ulysse Nardin joined forces with Urwerk to unveil the UR-Freak, one of the most contemporary iterations of luxury watchmaking in recent times.

Industry observers note that consumers reflected these sentiments in our 2026 survey. When asked, “Which developments excite you the most in the luxury watch market?”, the top three answers were: limited-edition watches, resale service and experiences. Excitement around resale services was consistent across age groups, with a median value of 60% — the lowest recorded value was among Gen Z (18-24) at 56.4% and the highest among boomers (55-64) at 65.5%.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, 70% of luxury watch consumers globally are excited about limited-edition watches, with this rising to 76% among Chinese shoppers. When it comes to experiences, 58% globally are most excited about these novel ways to experience brands, especially 25- to 34-year-olds, at 66%.

Sources indicate that longines has risen to the top 10 in the Vogue Business Watch Index this year (seeing a 58% increase), thanks to a combination of niche sports and celebrity tie-ins. The brand’s performance was helped by its long-time partnerships with equestrian competitions, which this year enjoyed extra visibility through the digital game Longines League of Nations™ Memory Game, developed in partnership with Fédération Équestre Internationale (FEI). The Commonwealth Games, which take place every four years and of which Longines was a sponsor, offered another boost. Longines’s astute partnerships are also noteworthy. Alongside its long-standing relationships with Jennifer Lawrence and Kate Winslet, the brand has partnered with rising Thai talent, gaining visibility in a country where Swiss watches have grown by 8.6% in value between January and September 2026 vs the same period in 2025.

Meanwhile, “Wes Anderson: The Archives”, the exhibition held at the Design Museum in London between November 2025 and July 2026 and dedicated to the filmmaker and long-time ambassador, was one of the factors that helped Hamburg-headquartered Montblanc improve its innovation score. Another factor was the #LetsWrite campaign, which transformed some of Montblanc’s flagship stores worldwide into oases to rediscover the art of writing. The visibility of these novel initiatives propelled the brand to sixth place, up 36 percentage points.

Montblanc’s partnership with long-time ambassador Wes Anderson, celebrated in the Design Museum’s “Wes Anderson: The Archives” exhibition, helped the brand climb to sixth place for innovation.

Sources indicate that panerai and Piaget both grew by 16%, earning their positions in the top 10. Panerai’s brand exhibition in its hometown of Florence boosted the brand’s score, along with customer services such as virtual try-ons. The collaboration with The Andy Warhol Foundation, an innovative use of a Snapchat lens for virtual try-on, and the offer of a digital product passport (DPP) are some of the factors behind Piaget’s progress.

In a recent development, at the top of the table, despite a few shuffles, last year’s best performers broadly maintained their positions this year. Breitling takes the crown with 11 percentage points of growth, jumping two positions ahead of IWC and Cartier, which in 2026 occupied second and third place, respectively. Chopard sits in fourth alongside Panerai, which records a substantial 16% increase in fifth position, up three positions vs. 2025. Hublot slips to sixth, down from fourth last year.

More shifts have happened at the bottom of the table. Although Patek Philippe and Tudor remain among the bottom five, Zenith marks a standout recovery with an increase of 26 percentage points, alongside Rolex, which has moved up by 10 percentage points.

Both Movado and A. Lange & Söhne have lost about 10 percentage points, moving down among the bottom 10 brands, alongside Omega, which has fallen 20 percentage points and landed in the bottom five. Despite its collaboration with Swatch for the Audemars Piguet x Swatch Royal Pop Collection, the Le Brassus-headquartered brand dropped 26 percentage points, losing five positions and landing in the middle of the table at 11th place.

Sources indicate that seismic shifts in the watch industry have prompted brands to sign a latest cohort of celebrity ambassadors who can seduce audiences in promising new markets. While China’s economic landscape still keeps imports in negative territory, and the war in Iran has disrupted the Middle East market, with Saudi Arabia’s market contracting by 10.3%, India, South Korea and Thailand are growing.

In June 2026, Rolex grabbed headlines not with one of its many leading tennis players at Roland-Garros but with the appointment of Priyanka Chopra Jones as its first Indian entertainment celebrity to join its roster of “testimonees” — the brand’s lingo for ambassadors. The brand had previously signed only Indian athletes, including tennis player Vijay Amritraj and golfers Jeev Milkha Singh and Anirban Lahiri. This move acknowledges the growing importance of the Indian market in the watchmaking business. According to the Federation of the Swiss Watch Industry, the value of Indian imports of timepieces grew by 28.5% in 2026 vs 2025 (January–September) and by 40.9% vs 2024 (January–September).

Other watch brands have also signed up Indian celebrities: Omega appointed javelin thrower Neeraj Chopra, and Rado teamed up with female cricketer Smriti Mandhana.

It has been revealed that in the wake of Thailand’s rise in the watch business, brands have been signing up Thai talents in rapid succession. This summer, Cartier added actor PP Krit Amnuaydechkorn to its portfolio of Thai ambassadors, which already includes singer and actor Jeff Satur, actress Kimberley Anne Woltemas, and actor Tor Thanapob Leeratanakachorn. Meanwhile, Piaget has teamed up with Thai actor Apo Nattawin Wattanagitiphat since 2024, and Casio featured Thai kickboxing world champion Superbon Singha Mawynn in its “Tough Like You” campaign.

But a top priority for watch brands right now is having a South Korean talent, preferably from one of the bands riding high on K-pop mania. At the start of 2026, Hublot signed Jung Kook, a member of the beloved band BTS, who has over 27 million Instagram followers and 35 million on TikTok. Meanwhile, in 2025, Piaget appointed actress Gianna Jun, following in the footsteps of Longines, which the year before brought on board actress Bae Suzy, a former member of the K-pop girl group Miss A. Omega has three South Korean ambassadors: actress Shin Min-a and actors Park Bo-gum and Hyun Bin, while Chopard signed all four members of K-pop band Aespa — Karina, Winter, Giselle and Ningning — back in 2023.

Hublot signed Jung Kook, a member of the beloved band BTS, who has over 27 million Instagram followers and 35 million on TikTok.

Watchmakers have also experimented with a different cohort of ambassadors: Ulysse Nardin’s tie-up with chef chocolatier Amaury Guichon led to approximately half a billion views across social media, according to the brand, while Gallet, a brand owned by Breitling, has partnered with a group of six explorers active on social media for its relaunch campaign.

In a recent development, the watch and automotive partnership is nothing new, thanks to the overlapping interests in mechanics, design and a predominantly male clientele, and recent collaborations suggest this is unlikely to change. Tag Heuer’s long-standing partnership with Formula 1 was boosted last year when LVMH took over the tournament sponsorship from Rolex, offering the brand the opportunity to further expand associated products and storytelling. Early this year, Breitling signed a global, multi-year partnership with Aston Martin, leading to the release of the Navitimer B01 Chronograph 43 Aston Martin Aramco, marking Breitling’s return to Formula 1. Bianchet revealed a partnership with Maserati, unveiling the first UltraFino Maserati at Watches and Wonders in Geneva. Meanwhile, Casio teamed up with Toyota Racing, and Roger Dubuis confirmed its enduring association with Lamborghini.

It has been revealed that but there have been some twists in the category. At the end of the summer, Seiko announced a collaboration with Honda — not with any of its cars or muscular motorcycles, but with Motocompo, a compact, foldable scooter — the very opposite of a bling, power-signaling motor vehicle. It was one of many recent unusual collaborations that watchmakers hope will reach latest audiences, unveil novel features of their brand’s DNA, and make them seem less intimidating and more approachable.

According to recent reports, at the end of 2025, Zenith collaborated with the furniture organization USM, whose designs are ubiquitous at Zenith’s headquarters in Le Locle, on a series of four Defy watches featuring USM’s saturated colors and delivered in USM boxes made with its signature Haller modular system. Rado entered into a similar partnership with the industrial design company Tej Chauhan.

In a recent development, more unusual still, in September this year, Casio unveiled a new AQ-230ECK with a distinctive matcha-tea-green dial featuring a black fox at 12 o’clock and, at 6 o’clock, the logo of Café Kitsuné, the coffee shop chain of French-Japanese brand Maison Kitsuné. This indicates the trend toward unlikely collaborators extends beyond the luxury end of the market and is taking root across the sector as a whole.

Industry observers note that another unlikely partnership was between German watchmaker Nomos and Doctors Without Borders, which aims to raise funds and awareness for the work of doctors in areas plagued by wars, natural disasters and epidemics, and to provide access to necessary health care. This partnership resulted in a limited-edition Ludwig model featuring a red number 12 on a white dial.

Recent findings suggest that even tried-and-tested art partnerships have lately taken on unexpected forms. At the end of last year, Roger Dubuis released a series of watches in collaboration with Los Angeles-based tattoo artist Dr Woo, while this year, Vacheron Constantin invited artists such as glass-makers and wood furniture designers to miniaturize their work to fit the proportions of a watch dial.

Meanwhile, Hublot grabbed headlines with two latest watches co-designed by artist Jeff Koons. The first is the Hublot Classic Fusion Balloon Dog, a series of three timepieces in red, blue and silver, each limited to 200 pieces, mimicking Koons’s iconic inflated dog sculpture in its rounded bezel, case and crown. The second is the more elaborate, gem-set Hublot MP-14 Origin inspired by Koons’s Gazing Ball works. In some ways, these standout partnerships make the high-profile, long-established relationship between Omega and the James Bond franchise — most recently leading to six new Seamaster Diver models inspired by James Bond and Spectre — seem quite tame in comparison.

Omega’s upcoming Seamaster Diver 300M Spectre edition. Released on Global James Bond Day, it’s the first time in the brand’s three-decade partnership with the franchise that Omega has made a watch for Bond’s nemesis.

During the watch fair Watches and Wonders in April, Swatch ran a newspaper ad that read, “The real wonders are happening in May.” What subsequently happened was the collaboration that dominated the news in 2026: the one between Audemars Piguet and Swatch for the release of the Royal Pop, the $439 pocket watch shaped like Audemars Piguet’s Royal Oak, made in the eye-popping colors and affordable materials of a Swatch timepiece.

Recent findings suggest that it marks the first time Swatch collaborated with a brand outside its portfolio, as previous tie-ups were with Omega for the MoonSwatch and Blancpain for Fifty Fathoms. It’s also the very first time Audemars Piguet released a watch bearing its logo and costing considerably less than $20,000, its usual entry price.

According to recent reports, the enthusiasm around the watch release was so exceptionally high that it led to people camping outside the authorized Swatch stores for days, marred by episodes of violence. “Everybody was so enthusiastic about this innovative product and the combination of two iconic Swiss brands in extremely opposite segments that they forgot the Royal Pop is not a product to be sold only on the launch day but over many months,” Swatch CEO Nick Hayek said, answering the criticism around the launch in an interview with Vogue Business.

It has been revealed that but the collaboration was still significant because it considerably boosted awareness of both brands and increased traffic to both their websites and social media accounts. Mr Hayek also hopes that the collaboration can reignite interest in more affordable watches in a climate where the industry keeps moving upmarket. “My father always said: be careful when an industry keeps moving further upmarket and becoming more expensive — you lose creativity, you lose innovation,” Hayek indicates. “It’s the same in many industries. If a luxury industry starts producing only for the elite, only for a small bubble of people, eventually billions of real people disconnect.”.

Double-signed watches have been a feature of the watch industry since its infancy, when a watch would bear the logo of the movement maker as well as that of the retailer. In the vintage market, double-signed timepieces such as Audemars Piguet-Tiffany or Patek Philippe-Cartier are sought-after rarities. But as watchmakers progressively chose to produce their own movements, double-signed watches disappeared. This new wave of watch brand collaborations aims not only to blend design and storytelling to appeal to a much wider audience, but also to combine elements of the brands’ own movements to intrigue watch nerds.

What have you done to bring your brand closer to women?

We believe our roots in technique and our passion for precision are genderless and can appeal to both men and women. Women have always been part of the brand’s history, as the jewelry watches in our archive prove. We have never wanted to create a separate universe and products specifically for women. Instead, we have worked on our products, the design of our boutiques, and our communications.

Sources indicate that we have expanded our product range to include more ergonomic case sizes, giving clients the freedom to choose proportions that best suit their wrists and personal style. We have also focused on making our boutique design aesthetically appealing and welcoming for both men and women. And finally, communication has been crucial. Female ambassadors, such as supermodel Gisele Bündchen and Eileen Gu, have also hugely helped raise our brand awareness among women.

IWC ambassador Gisele Bündchen.

How has your loyalty to Formula 1 played out in your strategy?

Formula 1, and motorsport in general, has always been part of our identity, and we continue to show that loyalty through our ambassadors, George Russell and Kimi Antonelli. Our affinity for Formula 1 led to last year’s collaboration with F1 The Movie.

Recent findings suggest that our loyalty to Formula 1 is also helping the brand raise its profile among women. In the past, the Formula 1 audience was 80% men and only 20% women. The balance is now 50-50, meaning more women have grown closer to our brand thanks to Formula 1. A case in point is our fresh friend of the brand, George Russell’s fiancée, Carmen Montero Mundt, who spontaneously began wearing our brand. It often happens that our clients’ wives also like the brand, and entire generations often become loyal clients.

How have you employed social media to draw women closer?

Industry observers note that our social media channels help us connect with women. On our channels, we regularly show famous women and models wearing our watches, as well as the women working in our manufacture. Last year, we debuted the series “IWC.Inspired”, which celebrates the achievements of women from all walks of life who use time wisely and with purpose. So far, we have featured skincare expert Melanie Grant, Michelle Kennedy, founder of the social networking app Peanut, and British model and entrepreneur Jodie Kidd.

The Vogue Business Watch Index assigns an innovation score to the experiences and services brands offer to existing clients, prospective ones and stakeholders at large across the digital and physical worlds.

The services examined in the digital world include NFTs, augmented reality and virtual reality on brands’ websites and social media channels that allow virtual try-ons or immersive, game-like experiences; collaborations across films, TV and gaming; and the digital translation of physical experiences such as exhibitions.

Among the services assessed in the physical world are traceability tools, resale services offered either directly by the brand or a third party, the acceptance of cryptocurrency payments, and virtual consultations straddling the digital and physical realms.

According to recent reports, consumer research was conducted over October 2026, while digital data and innovation audit data captured the period between September 2025 and August 2026. Data was captured across 20 brands and metrics are weighted according to the importance assigned by survey respondents.

#112003. The Carnivore Diet Is Peak Protein Extremism. How Healthy Is It Really?

The Carnivore Diet Is Peak Protein Extremism. How Healthy Is It Really?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1369 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You know your obsession with protein has gone too far when you’re waiting in line at Erewhon for a raw meat smoothie.
  • Eating raw organs is a step too far, but maybe you’ve heard about the benefits of the carnivore diet and you’re curious.
  • According to recent reports, maybe plant-based eating leaves you gassy and unsatisfied.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You know your obsession with protein has gone too far when you’re waiting in line at Erewhon for a raw meat smoothie. The speciality drink was created by Paul Saladino, who regularly preaches the benefits of following an animal-based diet. If you look inside the blender, you’ll find kefir, beef organs (like liver, heart, kidney, and spleen from Saldino’s Heart & Soil line), and “immunomilk,” which is freeze-dried cow’s colostrum. Yum. Saladino may be an outlier, but he certainly isn’t the only person pushing a meat-heavy diet. Brian Johnson, aka the “liver king,” follows an extreme ancestral carnivore diet, eating a pound of raw liver a day.

Eating raw organs is a step too far, but maybe you’ve heard about the benefits of the carnivore diet and you’re curious. According to a 2026 study published in Nutrients, the number of posts about the carnivore diet on Instagram is in the millions—and they didn’t even look at TikTok. Interest surrounding the carnivore diet has shown no signs of slowing down.

According to recent reports, maybe plant-based eating leaves you gassy and unsatisfied. You can’t help that you like wings. Before you take vegetables off the table completely, it’s crucial to know what the carnivore diet is and how it impacts health, both short-term and long-term. As experts explain here, it’s not all bad. But there are some important risks to be aware of.

It has been revealed that the aforementioned Nutrients study on the carnivore diet explains that there isn’t one standard definition of what the carnivore diet actually is, but generally speaking, it’s a diet where you only eat minimally processed animal foods, including organ meats, fish, seafood, eggs, animal fats, and full-fat dairy. Plant-based foods are eliminated entirely.

While eliminating foods like fruits, vegetables, and whole grains is extreme, Pouria Sefidmooye Azar, PhD, RD, a registered dietitian and assistant professor at the University of Central Arkansas, claims the carnivore diet isn’t all bad. He says that short term, many people lose weight eating this way.

Industry observers note that “Protein is more satiating than carbs and fats, so people following the carnivore diet often stay full for a longer amount of time, which means they reduce their caloric intake,” he says. Logically, it makes sense. If you’re eating foods like beef, chicken, and salmon, you’ll be less likely to dig into the pantry for snacks than if you ate a bowl of noodles.

In a recent development, dr. Azar states it’s notable not to conflate weight loss with getting healthier. He says that by eliminating plants, you’re going to miss out on a lot of important nutrients the body needs. You can probably guess the big one. Yep, fiber. “"If you’re cutting out every plant food, you're not getting fiber or phytonutrients, which are protective compounds found only in plants,” says Chris Vogliano, PhD, RD, a registered dietitian and global food systems expert.

It has been revealed that while you might not suffer any consequences of this immediately, both dietitians say that continuing to eat this way can mess up your digestion. You need fiber for good poops, plain and simple. Dr. Azar claims that we also need fiber to feed the healthy gut bacteria in the microbiome. This is important for supporting mental health, immune health, and minimizing the risk of chronic diseases and cancers.

Sources indicate that dr. Azar specifically calls out the connection between a high-meat, low-fiber diet and the risk of colorectal cancer. For example, a 2015 Oncology Reviews study shows a connection between red meat consumption and colorectal cancer risk, while a 2026 European Journal of Cancer study called low fiber consumption a major risk factor for colorectal cancer.

Sources indicate that considering that men are at increased risk for heart disease (the number one cause of death in the U.S.), it’s key to know how the carnivore diet can impact your cardiovascular health. Spoiler alert: It’s not good. “I would not recommend the carnivore diet as a healthy, long-term eating pattern,” says Sunny Intwala, MD, MBA, preventive cardiologist and the director of Prevention & Wellness at Northwell Health.

It has been revealed that dr. Intwala explains that this is because meat doesn’t just contain protein; it has a lot of saturated fat too. He says that diets centering around red meat increase LDL cholesterol and blood pressure in a few short weeks. This, he says, can contribute to inflammation and plaque buildup that increases the risk of heart attack and stroke.

As someone who studies how the way we eat impacts the planet, Dr. Vogliano points out that the carnivore diet is pretty horrible for the environment. “From a food systems lens, a meat-only diet on a global or even national level would carry massive environmental costs from land, water, and greenhouse gas emissions. This is regardless of whether the meat is conventionally raised, organic, or even regenerative. There’s just not enough land to produce that much meat,” he states.

According to recent reports, okay, we need plants. But what about the Brian Johnsons and Paul Salidinos of the world preaching the benefits of eating raw meat? If you are going to eat meat, are there benefits to eating it raw?

Recent findings suggest that both dietitians say no, emphasizing that there is no scientific evidence showing that raw meat is more beneficial in any way than eating cooked meat. “Liver is a nutrient-rich food and a great way to get vitamin A, vitamin B12, folate, and iron. But you can get that from cooked liver; you don’t have to eat it raw,” Dr. Vogliano claims. In fact, he emphasizes that eating any meat raw increases the risk of foodborne illnesses like Salmonella and E.coli.

Dr. Azar warns against pulling a Rocky and eating raw eggs either. “The protein in raw eggs is between 50 and 60% digestible. But the protein digestibility in cooked eggs is over 90%,” he says. A study from the ‘90s in The Journal of Nutrition backs this up.

It’s worth noting that this isn’t the same for meat. A 2015 study in the same journal found that the cooking time for meat didn’t impact protein digestibility very much. So while you may get the same amount of digestible protein from raw meat as you would cooked meat, your risk of foodborne illness is greater.

Decades of scientific research make it clear that a plant-free diet is not a healthy diet. If you’re a meat lover, you might be wondering just how much meat you can get away with eating without compromising your health.

It has been revealed that dr. Azar’s advice is this: Meat can still be your primary protein source. Just eat some plants along with it. “If you love meat, you can still eat foods like beef and chicken, but you also need to eat fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and nuts and seeds because there are some nutrients you just can’t get from meat,” he indicates, adding that only eating meat will lead to nutrient deficiencies.

Sources indicate that dr. Vogliano delivers a dietary message you’ve likely heard many times before: The healthiest diet is a diverse one. “We know from scientific research that the more plant foods our diets consist of, the more insurance we have that we’re getting the nutrients the body needs,” he says. Because of this, he advocates for a primarily plant-based diet and only eating meat occasionally.

Different governing bodies have slightly different recommendations when it comes to how much meat you can eat while still maintaining a healthy diet. The American Institute for Cancer Research says to keep red meat under 18 ounces a week, or roughly three portions a week. The American Heart Association doesn’t give a specific serving recommendation for meat, but says to mostly get protein from plants, fish, and seafood.

Dr. Azar emphasizes that there isn’t one universal way of eating that works for everyone. One diet may make one person feel energized and leave someone else feeling exhausted. What is important, he indicates, is making sure you’re getting all the nutrients your body needs. And what we know for sure is that you can’t do that by just eating meat.

#112002. Tech Report: Why Luxury Watch Brands Are Still Struggling Online

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2573 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Vogue ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Why Luxury Watch Brands Are Still Struggling Online

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2573 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The ever-shifting digital landscape rewards brands that are creative, agile, consistent across geographic areas, and can turn digital awareness into commercial opportunities through an effective omnichannel strategy.
  • However, traditional discovery channels are proving resilient in the watch industry.
  • In our digital analysis for the 2026 Vogue Business Watch Index, while the crown once again goes to Cartier, the ranking shows several changes and surprises, notably IWC’s rise and Rolex’s slide.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The ever-shifting digital landscape rewards brands that are creative, agile, consistent across geographic areas, and can turn digital awareness into commercial opportunities through an effective omnichannel strategy. In this competitive environment, small brands with a focused, strategic approach can appear larger than life, while market leaders resting on their laurels could see their relevance shrink.

However, traditional discovery channels are proving resilient in the watch industry. Brand-owned websites remain the top destination for information and upcoming brand or product discovery, despite the rise of social media. The challenge is to turn digital visibility into engagement through strong direct-to-consumer (DTC) websites and a seamless omnichannel experience.

In our digital analysis for the 2026 Vogue Business Watch Index, while the crown once again goes to Cartier, the ranking shows several changes and surprises, notably IWC’s rise and Rolex’s slide. Due to the unavailability of data this year, Vogue Business has removed its review of performance on Chinese social media platforms WeChat, Xiaohongshu and Weibo as part of its methodology patch. And while brands continuously refine their tactics on well-established — yet always evolving — digital platforms, it’s also crucial to track emerging ones that are rapidly capturing the public’s attention.

It has been revealed that in this year’s index, Hublot delivers a standout performance, jumping seven positions in the digital ranking vs. 2025 and landing just outside the top five. The key contributors to Hublot’s ascent are its robust digital services, which include a comprehensive omnichannel experience, and its Instagram performance. The brand has seen follower and engagement growth through content created in collaboration with its roster of ambassadors spanning sports and art.

IWC has considerably strengthened its position in the top five, advancing three places and landing second behind Cartier, thanks to exceptional social media performance, particularly on Facebook, where its engineering- and Formula 1-focused content continues to resonate. Omega slipped one place to third, yet remained a strong digital performer. The brand is strong on Instagram, TikTok and WeChat, and its Google Search visibility has increased year-on-year.

Meanwhile, despite its strong awareness and about 185 million Google visits from September 2025 to August 2026, Rolex slipped from third place in 2025 to fifth this year, due to insufficient activity, particularly on TikTok, where the brand has over 230,000 followers.

Recent findings suggest that longines’s fall from fourth to ninth place stands out. Historically, it’s a brand that performed well on Chinese platforms like Xiaohongshu and WeChat. However, its modest visibility on Western social media channels drags down its overall performance this year and highlights the need to deliver a consistent message across all geographies.

A granular analysis of the overall digital ranking unveils that each brand has its own specific strengths and weaknesses. Yet a dichotomy emerges between brands with strong digital visibility and those that can integrate that digital visibility into omnichannel customer service activities that may ultimately lead to commercial transactions.

The brands that perform best for digital, for example with high levels of engagement and interaction, are not always the brands that consumers rate highly for digital experience. For the most part, our consumer research demonstrates that opinions of content generally lag behind a more positive perception of the overall digital experience, with Tudor showing the biggest gap between the two.

It has been revealed that although Hublot ranks sixth in the overall digital ranking, it still has room to improve its omnichannel digital services. The brand boasts an innovative club-like loyalty program known as Hublotista, open to all Hublot watch owners; it offers live chats and click-and-collect options. However, other elements, such as product personalization and live inventory availability, trail competitors. Hublot is also the top performer on Instagram, but it ranks 15th in its Google Search traffic score. This means the brand excels at creating visibility and capitalizing on it through services, but it still has room to improve its equity in overall desirability.

While Omega sits at 89% and third in the digital ranking, its omnichannel services have significant scope for growth. Although it has several customer service options, some more dynamic offerings, like loyalty programs, live inventories, and product customization, could be strengthened. In contrast, Panerai performs well on omnichannel for a brand of its size, coming in third for this assessment with its Panerai Passport service, WhatsApp customer service option and strong online-offline integration, but its digital performance on socials is significantly behind others, putting it at 18th overall for digital. Meanwhile, Richemont-owned Piaget ranks 16th overall for digital, driven by poorer exposure on Google Search and TikTok, but places fifth for omnichannel with a strong range of customer service options, click-and-collect and pre-order options.

But it’s Rolex that indicates the most drastic dichotomy. The undisputed market leader, it generated a total turnover of CHF 11 billion ($13.1 billion) in 2025, up 4% from 2024, and commands a market share of 32.9%, followed by Cartier (8.7%), Patek Philippe (7%) and Omega (6.4%). The brand also tops the YouTube ranking and is the second most-searched brand on Google, behind Cartier. Yet while Rolex ranks fifth overall for digital performance, it is 17th for omnichannel services. Its absence from TikTok and limited digital services, which the brand typically hands over to its distributors rather than managing directly, weigh on its performance.

In a recent development, services generally rank high among respondents’ preferences. Real-time product availability both in-store and online is the most sought-after service for 79%, followed by multiple channels of customer service (email, phone, messenger) at 76%, buying from the brand’s website at 74%, and the ability to speak directly to a brand advisor (phone, video, live chat) when shopping online at 73%. The possibility to pay in local currency far outweighs cryptocurrency (70% vs 26%), although crypto matters more for 41% of older Gen Z and younger millennials aged 25-34. All the services highlighted imply the importance of human contact and physical presence, which are also common denominators for brand experiences — the other most important development that excites consumers (alongside limited-edition timepieces).

Since the early 2000s, when Google Search began to rise in the digital world, search engine optimization (SEO) has been front and center in brands’ digital preoccupations, ensuring their products are easily found on Google and placed at the top of consumers’ search results. Websites, e-commerce platforms and digital campaigns are now built to match SEO criteria. But Google’s dominance is eroding and, with it, the foundations of brands’ digital strategies are starting to wobble, as consumers flock to AI-driven chatbots where GEO (generative engine optimization) becomes the new metric to please.

The watch industry is still, by and large, a sector that relies on traditional modes of discovery. Brand websites are the top channel for both sourcing information and discovering new brands or products, highlighting how notable it is for brands to have robust DTC websites. This is reinforced by the fact that, on average across all brands, nearly half (47.8%) of consumers who purchased watches in the last year bought directly from the brand. When researching watches, word-of-mouth recommendations and review sites or discussion forums rank among the top five channels, alongside search engines and magazines.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to discovering upcoming products or brands, however, magazines and social media play an influential role, as do monobrand stores and flagships. Yet in the fast-changing digital landscape, new modes of discovery are becoming increasingly ingrained in shopping habits, and preferred purchasing channels are shifting, with the average number of people using resale rising from 29.7% who shopped in the last year to 40.8% of those intending to buy in the coming year.

It has been revealed that according to a Bain & Company study published in March, 56% of US-based consumers still resort to Google, but 16% already mostly or always use AI chatbots and 28% mix the two. But adoption of AI chatbots is stronger among Gen Z (25% mostly or always use chatbots and 33% mix the two), millennials (24% mostly or always use chatbots and 34% mix the two), and Gen X (14% mostly or always use chatbots and 31% mix the two). Thirty-three per cent of consumers already use AI chatbots for recommendations in general and 19% for shopping assistance specifically.

In this context, some brands have started to adapt. Nomos Glashütte, an independent watch brand based in the German watchmaking cluster that is also home to Richemont-owned A. Lange & Söhne, has begun updating its website to ensure AI chatbots can read it correctly and surface the brand’s products in their recommendations.

Analysts consider a website overhaul the easiest component of GEO brands can act on; the others remain much harder to control. AI chatbots draw information not only from brands’ websites but also from articles published in legacy media, typically sorted by readership and prestige. This is an element brands can influence through old-school public relations activity, but it is not fully under their sway. The third component is even more elusive: consumers’ comments on social media.

While brands practice “social listening” to improve on public feedback, they still can’t control people’s opinions and messages. But such comments are increasingly finding their way into AI chatbots, and they predominantly come from social media that are still latest territory for brands: Reddit and Substack.

According to recent reports, A 2025 survey of Gen Zs, conducted by Vogue Business and youth culture agency Archrival, found that 65% of respondents use Reddit to find and discover products, valuing the platform’s privacy and the ability to ask questions anonymously. Vogue Business also highlighted that customers typically spend longer on Reddit’s detailed threads than they do on other social platforms.

It has been revealed that AI visibility is rapidly gaining relevance. Launchmetrics introduced a fresh AI Visibility metric alongside its usual proprietary Media Impact Value. According to the firm’s analysis of brand mentions by AI during the Watches and Wonders fair, “being liked and being mentioned are two different things in AI. Tudor and Panerai come up far less often in AI answers, but when they do appear, they’re described so positively that it impacts their overall rank to third and fourth overall.”.

Industry observers note that IWC achieves an impressive 95% score and lands in second place in the digital marketing ranking behind Cartier, as its laser-focused video strategy, highlighting a few key messages, delivers significant results. The Schaffhausen-headquartered brand is best-performing on Facebook with a score of 93%; second best on TikTok with 90%, behind Cartier (95%); and on YouTube with 89%, behind Rolex (92%).

The brand’s message, anchored in engineering excellence and innovation, is articulated through its association with Formula 1 and a few well-selected ambassadors who don’t simply pose wearing a timepiece but get involved in brand-related projects. IWC also regularly features videos of its watchmakers assembling timepieces. One filming Florian Salzer working on the Ingenieur Tourbillon 41 IWC345901 amassed over 10 million views and over half a million likes on TikTok alone.

IWC also runs the successful series “IWC Replies”, in which watchmakers answer technical questions asked by the community, like “Would the perpetual calendar still work after 2299?”.

This year, IWC released a series of timepieces co-designed with George Russell, a driver for the Mercedes-AMG Petronas Formula 1 team. The watch was made in the racing team’s blue hue, engraved on the back with Russell’s number 63, and Russell himself featured in the social media campaign. The brand has previously collaborated with supermodel Gisele Bündchen, who was not only an ambassador but an environmental and community projects advisor. The brand playfully mixes engineering-focused content with ambassador-led storytelling. One TikTok video featuring Russell’s teammate, Kimi Antonelli, assembling a timepiece achieved half a million views, proving the appeal of involving the brand’s “myth-makers” in the watchmaking process.

Videos of IWC’s watchmakers at work have helped the brand rise three places to second in this year’s Index.

IWC also explores content related to travel where precision matters, like space travel and aviation. This year, the brand is collaborating with Vast to test timepieces during space flights. In a more poetic vein, the brand also released a upcoming Pilot’s Watch celebrating the 20th anniversary of its association with the foundation linked to author and aviator Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, who wrote the children’s tale of the space traveler The Little Prince.

Managing director, Ulysse Nardin.

Industry observers note that while many watchmakers still value traditional media, Ulysse Nardin has embraced social media and made it a pillar of its communications strategy. Why?

It has been revealed that continuous improvement is obviously a must, but in brand-building, it is not enough. There are many elements of brand-building we could choose to focus on, but not all would deliver the same impact. With all the money in the world, I don’t think we could revolutionize the in-store customer experience and move the needle for our brand.

Sources indicate that but social media is still a blue ocean, in the sense that small investments can deliver impactful, meaningful results. But you need to know the rules of the game. The type of content that is consumed and thrives on social media is made by content creators, not the polished content by luxury brands. People relate to people, and partnering with content creators is paramount.

We asked ourselves: how can we go viral and put our iconic Freak watch in the minds of millions of people with minimal investment?

Sources indicate that we noticed that food-related content was getting a lot of traction, so we decided to collaborate with chocolate specialist Amaury Guichon, who is half Swiss and half French. The video of him making a giant chocolate sculpture of the Freak watch was watched by half a billion people. Amaury Guichon is now a friend of the brand, and we featured him in our UNstoppable campaign on social media, which celebrates the achievements of extraordinary people.

And you managed to have a massive impact at Watches and Wonders with dancing robots. Tell us more about that.

One of the brand’s pillars, which is transversal across all our activities, is our mission to inspire innovation.

Recent findings suggest that we knew that at Watches and Wonders, we did not want to be confined to a box and mark our presence on the whole fair. Renting two robots, which cost us less than a page of advertising in a glossy magazine, proved a very effective way to achieve our objective. We dressed them in sweaters celebrating the 25th anniversary of the Freak watch. As they greeted guests and danced, many visitors stopped to take pictures of them and share them on social media. The visitors became our spontaneous content creators.

Ulysse Nardin’s dancing robots at Watches and Wonders cost less than a magazine ad page and turned visitors into the brand’s content creators.

In a recent development, we spent no money on advertising at Watches and Wonders, but we had a big impact. Thanks to these unconventional actions, the Freak watch has become a pillar of the brand, accounting for about 50% of total turnover.

The Vogue Business Watch Index examines watchmakers’ digital activity across 48 social media platforms: the Western trinity of Facebook, Instagram and YouTube as well as the global China-native TikTok. Latest Update: The Tucson Restaurant Turning Cactus Into Fine Dining
