⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, traipsing through Tucson Mountain Park, a Midwestern blow-in might not identify much to eat.
  • Sources indicate that gray, tangled brittlebush, which the average Tucsonan walks or drives by almost daily, can be pressure-cooked, caramelized until black, and baked into cake.
  • In a recent development, don’t even get Lopez started on the dozens of cacti varieties that thrive here, which the restaurant sources from local grower Toadlet Farm and which Lopez harvests throughout the year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, traipsing through Tucson Mountain Park, a Midwestern blow-in might not identify much to eat. Plants armed with burs, barbs, and spines all but scream “do not touch.” For chef Aaron Lopez and June Chee, however, this prickly, dusty landscape stocks a pantry of possibility. The married co-owners of Ursa see the Arizona desert as a rich ground for foraging.

Sources indicate that gray, tangled brittlebush, which the average Tucsonan walks or drives by almost daily, can be pressure-cooked, caramelized until black, and baked into cake. Dusty, sage-colored salt bush, when hung to dry, takes on an intensely umami, aquatic saltiness like seaweed. The sweet buds of the Seussian-green palo verde tree become briny, like olives, when suffused with lye.

In a recent development, don’t even get Lopez started on the dozens of cacti varieties that thrive here, which the restaurant sources from local grower Toadlet Farm and which Lopez harvests throughout the year. The restaurant processes the young and mature paddles, fruit and their seeds, buds, and flowers, which are then grilled, poached, cold-smoked, juiced, dehydrated, nixtamalized, or preserved into jam, wine, and vinegar.

There are hundreds of edible plants in the Sonoran Desert. Ursa strives to showcase their potential, one 10-course meal at a time.

According to recent reports, “We treat Ursa as an art showroom, demonstrating to people what these plants can do, what sustainable means, and what was here before it got easy,” says Lopez. The idea was inspired in part by his Sonoran grandfather, Hector Lopez, who died in the spring. “He was the first person I ever heard say they’re proud to be from the desert,” the chef said.

Ursa began as a pop-up in California in 2023. Lopez and Chee moved to a historic brick building in downtown Tucson, re-opening their doors in October 2025. It’s a homecoming of sorts for the couple, who are both from the Sonoran Desert borderlands. They met in Hawaii, where Chee was working in clean energy and transportation. Lopez, meanwhile, spent roughly 18 years cooking in fine dining and modern progressive restaurants like Redbird and Orsa & Winston in LA, and Pai Honolulu. But he was longing for the desert.

After helping a friend open a restaurant and hosting a few popups in Austin, Lopez and Chee bought a desert foraging guide, packed up their two dogs and began driving around the Southwest. It made sense to settle in Tucson, which was recognized by UNESCO in 2015 as a Creative City of Gastronomy for its continuous 4,000-year agricultural history and deeply rooted Sonoran Desert food traditions.

“That’s a unique thing about being here, the connection from seed to plant to restaurant that we hadn’t been able to grasp before,” Chee says.

Recent findings suggest that consider a recent course that Ursa built around tepary beans, in which the ancient, nutty bean is refried and topped with h:al squash that’s been lactofermented. The squash’s leaves are fermented to make Japanese-style kosho and its flowers are pickled, dried, crushed with dried saltbush, then tossed with barrel cactus seeds for a desert furikake. It’s served with grilled coins of chorizo made from Lopez’s great-grandmother’s recipe and housemade flour tortillas, to all be washed down with an amazake drink made from fermented wheat and goat fat. Don’t get too attached, however. Riffs owing to finicky ingredient availability occur here almost daily.

Running a restaurant using only ingredients foraged and farmed from within about eight to 10 miles means abiding by pretty intense guardrails. The only wheat used is pima club, an ancient soft white variety cultivated for centuries by the Akimel O’odham (Pima) people. Ursa does not use cucumbers, radishes or citrus.

Industry observers note that “We’re not trying to substitute anything, like, ‘How do we achieve cucumber? Let’s grab a cactus,’” Lopez indicates. “We have to throw everything out, really strip it down. Sometimes we have to let the ingredients be bitter or spicy. We have to put our egos aside and let the ingredient be the star.”.

For staff who didn’t grow up or learn to cook here, the learning curve at Ursa can feel a little like alighting on a new planet, even if certain flora happen to resemble prickly weeds in their own backyards.

“We have these really cool moments in the restaurant where people are like, Oh! I have lamb’s quarter just growing in my yard!” Chee indicates of the spinach-like desert green that appears all over Ursa’s menu.

A young Aaron Lopez with his grandfather Hector Lopez.

Ursa’s approach isn’t always easy for customers to understand, so the couple came up with a more down-to-earth option. This fall, the restaurant debuted a four-course, family-style Lineage menu for $75, alongside the existing 10-course Harvest menu ($150). There’s now a pozole course inspired by the family’s annual springtime tradition of roasting goat in agave leaves, barbacoa-style, and shredding it for soup, and a red masa tamal with glazed quail and yucca blossoms in mole made with burnt mesquite bread, a technique Lopez remembers from childhood.

The idea took shape during Ursa’s extended summer break, as Lopez recovered from foot surgery and reflected on the loss of his late grandfather, the tenacious keeper of family traditions.

“I feel so much closer to my ancestors and the land; we want Ursa to be less esoteric and more soulful,” he notes. “The story of Ursa is partly of the desert, partly my family. Now we’ve advanced to the point where they’re symbiotic, and I can't tell them apart.”.

At a Stanford economic summit in 2024, Huang offered up a very practical, Silicon Valley-esque reason for his leather preference: They don’t make him itch. But they also felt like an intentional effort to use fashion to break beyond the tech industry’s traditionally geeky image, à la Mark Zuckerberg sitting front row at Prada or Adam Mosseri showing up at the Met Gala in Kartik Research.

Rather than evoking the likes of James Dean or Marlon Brando, the lush outerwear instead began to suggest a man in the throes of a midlife crisis.

According to recent reports, huang’s return as CEO isn’t unprecedented. For example, OpenAI’s Sam Altman was reinstated after employees revolted against the board’s initial firing of the CEO. The move does, however, raise concerns about national security and Nvidia’s firm culture.

The dismissal of the leather jacket marks a new chapter in Huang’s tenure at the helm of Nvidia. It had always been a talking point, and after becoming a symbol of his fall from grace, wearing it again would risk turning it into his own scarlet letter. By swapping out stiff leather for easy, approachable cotton, Huang seems to be signaling the desire for a reset. As he told his staff during his return: “I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around.”.

Who Topped the 2026 Vogue Business Watch Index?

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Following a challenging 2025, 2026 has offered some green shoots for the luxury watch industry.
  • Overall Swiss export value has grown by 2.7%, driven by unexpected pockets of growth in emerging markets (India +28.5%, Thailand +8.6% and Mexico +6.2%), which offset drops in traditionally strong markets like China (-5.9%) and Saudi Arabia (-10.3%).
  • Recent findings suggest that the digital audit highlights how brands are appointing high-profile cultural influencers in newer markets, from K-pop stars to Thai actors, as brand ambassadors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Following a challenging 2025, 2026 has offered some green shoots for the luxury watch industry.

Overall Swiss export value has grown by 2.7%, driven by unexpected pockets of growth in emerging markets (India +28.5%, Thailand +8.6% and Mexico +6.2%), which offset drops in traditionally strong markets like China (-5.9%) and Saudi Arabia (-10.3%). The latest consumer research from Vogue Business highlights nuanced market trends, underscoring the need for watch brands to pay particular attention to local cultural needs. In China, for example, despite a broader market slowdown, 55% of luxury watch consumers surveyed have bought themselves a timepiece to celebrate their birthday. Recognizing these behaviors can help brands make their messaging more impactful — a strategy that will become increasingly important as shoppers rely more on emerging channels to discover products and brands.

Recent findings suggest that the digital audit highlights how brands are appointing high-profile cultural influencers in newer markets, from K-pop stars to Thai actors, as brand ambassadors. As the geography of growth shifts, so too must campaign strategies.

According to recent reports, and while mainstream sports like motoring and equestrianism have historically provided key partnerships for luxury watches, more niche sports are helping brands reach upcoming audiences. Yet our digital analysis also exposes some tensions the industry is grappling with; the channels relied on for sourcing trusted information are not always the channels consumers use to discover new brands and products and, as use of generative AI becomes more widespread, brands will need to adapt their digital strategies to boost visibility in this emerging space. Opportunities also remain to strengthen the omnichannel experience, with our survey highlighting shopper frustration over limited online service options.

According to recent reports, in a market steeped in tradition, established leaders have defended their positions in the ranking, while collaborations with the worlds of film and art are helping legacy brands stay fresh. Consumers also continue to favor buying directly from brands, with 47.8% on average having bought their most recent watches this way or from multibrand specialists (22.5% on average). Yet while brand awareness has risen year on year, purchase intent remains relatively flat, even as enthusiasm for resale grows. As much as the availability of digital product passports (DPPs) and authentication services may encourage shoppers to engage with resale platforms, economic pressures expose a bigger driver: price sensitivity. Older consumers are particularly likely to wait for sales and discounts before making a purchase. This suggests that the demand for innovation in the pre-loved watch environment is as much a reflection of price sensitivity as it is the result of improved services in this space. It also means that, over the coming year, luxury watch brands will need to work harder to defend those “brand new” watch sales in the primary market.

Cartier retains its leadership position for the third year. This summer, Cartier added actor PP Krit Amnuaydechkorn to its portfolio of Thai ambassadors, which already includes singer and actor Jeff Satur, actress Kimberley Anne Woltemas and actor Tor Thanapob Leeratanakachorn. This has helped it to maintain momentum on platforms like Instagram and gain ground on TikTok. Yet while awareness has risen, consumer opinion is more mixed, with small declines in perception of innovation, value for money and experience, showing even leaders cannot rest on their laurels.

Sources indicate that improved consumer perception, the highest recognition and highest purchase intent have helped Rolex to secure the second spot in this year’s ranking. The availability of certified pre-owned Rolexes at official stockists means the brand is well-positioned to take advantage of the rising demand for pre-loved luxury timepieces. Small but steady gains on all Western social media platforms have also helped the brand to stay front of mind for consumers in a cluttered digital landscape.

Omega narrowly misses out on second place this year. The brand benefits from high awareness and improved perception across several metrics. Its strong digital performance is helped by high-profile collaborations, for example, its James Bond/Spectre partnerships, but the provision of omnichannel features and innovation performance leave room for growth.

After breaking into the top five last year, Tag Heuer has managed to hold on to fourth position. The brand benefits from significant gains in consumer awareness, perception of quality, and positive association with more emotional drivers, as well as increased purchase intent in a market where this is relatively flat. Against a backdrop of rising price sensitivity, its positioning may help it to weather a volatile economic period.

Sources indicate that after two years spent in sixth position, IWC moves into the top five for the first time this year. The brand ranks second for both Digital and Innovation, with a focused strategy on social media helping it reach fresh audiences. Its ongoing partnership with F1 is also helping to recruit more female followers, while its IWC.Inspired series celebrates women from all walks of life. Meanwhile, its partnership with Watchfinder enables consumers to part-exchange pre-loved IWC timepieces when making their next purchase, providing a seamless way to engage with the increasingly relevant resale market.

Twenty brands are assessed for the Vogue Business Watch Index, with brand performance evaluated against over 100 data points spanning consumer sentiment, digital marketing and innovation.

The weightings of each assessment category and their metrics are determined by industry relevance and importance to the consumer, allowing for an objective assessment of a brand’s performance. The final weighting for each category is agreed upon following a review process with our data analysts and expert editors. This year, we removed Chinese platforms from our digital audit due to lack of data availability, with weightings being reassigned proportionally to retained digital platforms (Facebook, Instagram, YouTube, TikTok and Google Search).

Consumer research remains fundamental to the Vogue Business Watch Index, with readers across several Condé Nast titles — including Vogue, GQ, Vanity Fair and Condé Nast Traveler — participating in an annual consumer sentiment survey that ensures granularity is achieved when it comes to understanding awareness, customer challenges and brand perception. This year, we surveyed 1,020 qualified luxury watch consumers in seven markets (the US, UK, France, Germany, Italy, the Middle East and China). Among them, 60% of luxury watch consumers spent between €1,500 and €4,999 on luxury watches in the last five years, while 40% spent over €5,000.

Future iterations of the Vogue Business Watch Index will continue to maximize the brands, metrics, and digital platforms assessed, with additions prioritized in line with industry needs and developments.

How One Live-Wire Stylist Puts His Meta Glasses to Work on Set

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Meta announced the latest generation of its genre-defining smart glasses, the response from the fashion industry was, well, kind of tepid. Wearable technology has a shaky track record, after all, and we’ve been down a similar road before. (Google Glass, we hardly knew thee.) To win over folks more fluent in Ai Weiwei than AI, Meta would have to fulfill a much trickier mandate than simply developing a groundbreaking product: it’d have to develop a product that looks good while doing the ground breaking.

So when I got the chance to put Meta Glasses to the test during a typically frenetic day on set shooting for GQ, I didn’t hold back. It helps, obviously, that they actually look cool—especially the limited-edition pair I requested, a collaboration with the chart-topping Blackpink member LISA. Now, though, I’m convinced of their genuine, potentially game-changing utility, too. Here’s how I put the Meta Glasses by LISA through the paces of my chaotic 9-to-5, and emerged all the less stressed for it.

According to recent reports, on shoot days, I make a point of arriving on set an hour before our model so I can lock in our looks with minimal distraction. The clothes on the racks, though, tend to play second fiddle to the clothes on me, at least when it comes to my AM fit check. (Like a true sicko, I wore a fluorescent Prada jacket to match the pink tint on my special-edition, LISA-designed Meta Glasses.).

It has been revealed that without fail, every shoot I’ve been on comes together very dynamically—read: absolutely last minute. So even though we boarded each look weeks ago, and styled them all out yesterday afternoon, no fewer than 15-ish items arrived that morning. To sort through them, I tell Meta to put on the latest Sophia Stel album so I can lock in and land on the right roster of looks.

Recent findings suggest that the looks have been landed on—it’s time to present them to the team. GQ commerce director Michael Nolledo—the magnanimous Miranda Priestly of the entire operation, if you will—is off-site for the day, so I tell Meta to video call him for approval. He can now see what I see, and I stay totally hands-free.

It has been revealed that during the run through, I describe each look down to its socks, clarifying the logic behind my styling decisions with near-comical specificity. (Yes, that minuscule sliver of waffle thermal peeking out from beneath that fleece is, in fact, transformative and entirely nonnegotiable!) I tend to love this part of the day because the looks always end up in a sometimes-different-always-better place once the braintrust has weighed in—and tempered some of my, uh, kookier impulses.

Sources indicate that it doesn’t matter how nice the clothes look hanging limply on the rack: they don’t really come to life (or die in front of your very eyes) until you get them on the guy. Luckily, our guy for the day is Gabriel, whose easy, unaffected chill makes everything we put him in look effortlessly incredible.

In a recent development, as we noodle on a few minor alternations (bringing in a suit jacket just-so; adding hefty cuffs to a pair of appropriately hefty trousers), I have Meta snap a photo of each look in its final form. On my command, Meta then sends those photos to Michael and GQ senior editor Avidan Grossman—my closest collaborator on set and our in-house tailoring geek—who has final say on all things pleated pants, dimpled ties, and more. Once Meta beams out the fitting photos, it’s speak now or forever hold your peace.

The next six hours are a frenetic blur, set to a fittingly chaotic blend of ‘80s pop hits and Tate McRae (it’s all about balance, really). Beth, our prodigiously talented photographer for the day, becomes my partner, as we both try to ensure Gabriel ignores the camera as much as possible. The best photos happen when the guy forgets he’s being photographed—like we’re capturing a genuine moment of relaxed solitude.

Problem is, when I’m laser-focused on all that, I hate pulling out my phone to capture content of my own. So the option to have Meta snap a fast photo or record a snippet of video is kind of a godsend.

We made it, folks. Three green teas, four minor hand injuries, and 18 or so looks later, it’s time for the fun part: reviewing the photos, and duking it out over which of them will make the final cut. There really is no greater satisfaction than seeing a slapdash deck of product flats transform into an all-killer, no-filler album of actual outfits.

It has been revealed that because I have no patience (and am beaming with so much pride it's nearly blinding), I have Meta snap a few shots of my favorite moments and then post them to my IG story. The official GQ story won’t run for a few weeks, so I like to think of my story as an unofficial teaser of sorts. We pack up and roll our racks out of the studio and back into the fashion closet, where I promptly ask Meta for directions to the closest bar.

In a recent development, and Garten has certainly gotten comfortable sharing the spotlight over the years. #111990. How to Make Whipped Cream Perfectly, Every Time

📅 27 Jul 2017 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1404 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bonappetit ↗ Open Full Page

How to Make Whipped Cream Perfectly, Every Time

📅 27 Jul 2017 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1404 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that if you love a low-effort, high-reward kitchen assignment, learning how to make whipped cream is a walk in the clouds.
  • In whipped cream, and in life, the key challenge is knowing when to stop.
  • To make whipped cream at home, all you need is cold heavy cream, a large bowl, and a whisk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if you love a low-effort, high-reward kitchen assignment, learning how to make whipped cream is a walk in the clouds. The only ingredients are time and heavy cream. You can use an electric mixer, a whisk, or a mason jar and strong-armed devotion.

In whipped cream, and in life, the key challenge is knowing when to stop. Desserts like Strawberry Eton Mess or Triple Chocolate Mousse Cake fare best with silky, unsweetened, soft-peaked whip. Others, like this show-stopping Berries and Cream Mille-Feuille, gain structure from sturdier peaks.

To make whipped cream at home, all you need is cold heavy cream, a large bowl, and a whisk. You can also use a handheld mixer or a mason jar and some elbow grease (more on that later).

It has been revealed that if you’re opting for a bowl-and-whisk combo, choose your tools wisely. Cream roughly doubles in volume as you whip it, so use a bowl with three to four times the capacity of your liquid. A large balloon whisk, rather than a narrow sauce whisk, helps incorporate plenty of air into the cream.

It has been revealed that be strategic in the dairy aisle too. Heavy cream and heavy whipping cream contain at least 36% milk fat and can be used interchangeably. Skip anything labeled simply “whipping cream”—or, heaven forbid, “light cream”—which contains less fat and won’t hold its loft as well.

Recent findings suggest that for a basic batch, start with 1 cup cold heavy cream, which makes about 2 cups whipped cream. For lightly sweetened whipped cream, add 1 Tbsp. powdered sugar; for vanilla whipped cream, add ½ tsp. vanilla extract or paste.

With your equipment and ingredients in hand, there are only five steps and infinite possibilities.

Because whipped cream is usually eaten with or as dessert, you might not need to sweeten it at all. To keep flavors balanced, we tend to serve whipped cream au naturel with Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie or Diner-Style Rice Pudding.

But there are no hard-and-fast rules. Maybe you love sweetened whipped cream, or you’re serving it with something less sugary—like, say, a bowl of tart blackberries and torn mint leaves.

Industry observers note that for lightly sweetened whipped cream, start with about 1 Tbsp. sugar per cup of cream. Powdered sugar dissolves easily and contains a little stabilizer (usually cornstarch), which can lend the whipped cream some extra holding power. Some cooks prefer the cleaner flavor of granulated sugar, which takes a little longer to dissolve. Either way, add the sugar before you start whipping.

According to recent reports, if you’re gazing at a bowl of fluffy, ethereal whip and thinking, “Could I make this even more enchanting?” the answer is yes. There are two primary ways to make flavored whipped cream: infuse or stir.

Kitchen professionals and advance planners tend to cold-infuse. Combine your cream with flavorings like rice (for a creamy Horchata) or bourbon (to take a classic pumpkin pie over the top), then store it in the fridge anywhere from three hours to overnight. Strain out any solids before whipping.

In a recent development, you can also add simple flavorings, like vanilla extract, a small splash of liqueur, cocoa, ground spices, citrus zest, or coffee syrup, before you start whipping. For heavier or chunky additions, such as toasted nuts or chopped chocolate, use a rubber spatula to gently fold them in once the cream is whipped.

Peaks are the shape your whipped cream takes when you pull the whisk out of the bowl and hold it upright like the Statue of Liberty’s torch.

Recent findings suggest that soft peaks are cloudlike and slump over when you lift the whisk. Stiff peaks stand upright and hold their shape. Somewhere in between are medium peaks, which have enough structure to hold a shape while remaining soft and supple.

Most Bon Appétit recipes, such as these Mix-and-Match Fools, involve whipping cream to soft peaks. That velvety texture is our go-to when we’re dolloping whipped cream atop pecan pie.

But we aren’t always such softies. Medium peaks help this Ginger-Raspberry Icebox Cake keep its shape. And old-fashioned chocolate mousse involves whipping batches of cream into stiff and soft peaks: The former is folded into the chocolate mixture for structure, while the softer stuff tops the dessert.

There’s more than one way to whip.

Sources indicate that by hand: Our preferred method, whipping cream by hand requires the most time and effort, but it also gives you optimal control over its final texture. Even if you use a mixer to get your whipped cream started, switching to a whisk for the final few moments makes it easier to stop exactly where you want.

In a recent development, in a Mason jar: No whisk? No mixer? No problem. To make whipped cream with your bare hands, put a container with a tight-fitting lid, large mason jar, or leak-proof cocktail shaker into the freezer for five minutes. Get the heavy cream very cold and make sure you have ample headspace in your vessel of choice. About one cup of liquid in a four-cup container is a good amount.

Secure the lid and shake it like you mean it. For the creamiest results, a consistently assertive pace is better than intermittent spurts of brute force. When the liquid stops sloshing and starts feeling and sounding heavier, open the lid and take a peek. If it looks underwhipped, close it back up and keep shaking.

In a recent development, good news for meal preppers: You can make whipped cream hours in advance. Err on the side of underwhipping it during your prep. Store the lightly whipped cream, covered, in the fridge for up to four hours before serving, then give it a few energetic whisks to bring back its bounce right before you dollop it onto dessert.

Recent findings suggest that you can also freeze whipped cream (no, seriously). It takes a bit of effort, though. Line a baking sheet with parchment, then pipe or scoop spoonfuls of whipped cream onto it. Freeze until the whipped cream nuggets are solid, then peel them off the parchment and store them in an airtight bag in the freezer for one to two months. When you’re ready to serve, let them thaw at room temperature for about 15 minutes.

Instant vanilla pudding is the key to luscious, long-lasting whipped cream.

Need it to hold up longer? Instant vanilla pudding mix is one of BA’s favorite shortcuts for stabilized whipped cream. For every cup of heavy cream, add 1 Tbsp. instant vanilla pudding mix (call it pastry cream powder if anyone gives you sass) and 2 tsp. powdered sugar, then whip as usual. The modified starch in the pudding mix absorbs excess moisture and helps prevent the cream from separating, keeping it fluffy for up to 24 hours.

It has been revealed that for something tangier, sour cream adds both flavor and body. Our Pecan Cream Pie whisks ¼ cup sour cream into 1 cup heavy cream; the sour cream cuts the richness while helping the topping hold its shape.

In any case, your dinner party guests don’t have to sit quietly as you furiously whisk their dessert topping to order. Prep work never tasted so sweet.

If your whip isn’t coming together quite right, don’t fret. Simple solutions abound.

This is probably a temperature issue. Cold cream whips more readily and holds onto the air you’re incorporating more effectively, so it comes together faster—and stays fluffy longer. Pop the bowl, whisk, and cream back into the freezer for five minutes, or into the fridge for up to 30. Once everything is cold, resume whisking.

Another possible culprit is the fat content of your cream. Opt for heavy whipping cream or heavy cream over half-and-half or other heavy cream substitutes.

If the cream is just a little too stiff or starting to look grainy, add a splash of chilled heavy cream and slowly whisk it in. Add more, a little at a time, until the texture smooths out.

Keep a close eye on it: If you whisk for too long, you’ll end up with a bowl of butter.

Editor’s note: This story was originally published in 2017 by Julia Black. It has been substantially updated with new reporting and additional advice from the Bon Appétit archives, including contributions by Amiel Stanek, Christina Chaey, Rochelle Bilow, and Elyssa Goldberg.

Industry observers note that thanksgiving is practically an Olympic event for eating, but there’s nothing wrong with a little warm-up the night before. Chipotle is bringing back its Thanksgiving Eve BOGO deal, giving you a perfectly good excuse to grab a burrito with an old friend before the turkey, stuffing, and inevitable food coma take over.

In a recent development, the deal runs Wednesday, November 25, from 5 to 9 p.m. local time at participating U.S. restaurants, with the usual buy one entrée, get one free format we all know and love.

It has been revealed that but, as expected, there’s some fine print worth reading before you get in line. You’ll need to be a Chipotle Rewards member, order at the restaurant, and scan your Rewards card at checkout. The free entrée must cost the same as or less than the one you're buying, and you can claim up to five free entrées per check. Kids’ meals don't qualify, and ordering ahead through the app, online, or for delivery won't work.

In a recent development, the timing has changed a bit from last year, too, when it ran from 4 p.m. all the way until closing. This time, you've got a four-hour window, so make sure that one friend you have who’s perpetually late gets the memo.

In a recent development, “The response last year showed us how much our guests embraced the occasion,” Stephanie Perdue, Chipotle's senior vice president of brand marketing, stated in a statement. According to the chain, the promotion ended up being its biggest sales-driving campaign of 2025, so a return trip was probably inevitable.

And if you’re stuffed and don’t feel like leaving the couch the next day, there’s a little something for the post-Thanksgiving crowd as well. From Friday, November 27, through Monday, November 30, Chipotle is waiving its delivery fee on eligible orders placed through its app or website with code CYBER26. You’ll need to spend at least $10 in the U.S. or $12 in Canada, and delivery menu prices may be higher, with other fees still applying.

If nothing else, it’s a convenient excuse to take a break from the annual challenge of finding increasingly creative ways to eat leftover turkey.

The Opera Coat Is Everywhere—Here’s the Chinese Influence Behind the Trend

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor.
  • It’s been living rent-free in my mind for the better part of this year: Conner Ives’s silk brocade opera coat, which captured nearly every fashion lover’s heart when it debuted on the fall/winter 2026 runway at London Fashion Week.
  • Recent findings suggest that the coat—crafted with silk tapestries dating back to the Qing dynasty and with hand-embroidered depictions of red-crowned cranes, bamboo leaves, and flowers—was undoubtedly the first wave in what would become a tsunami of a trend: opera coats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

It’s been living rent-free in my mind for the better part of this year: Conner Ives’s silk brocade opera coat, which captured nearly every fashion lover’s heart when it debuted on the fall/winter 2026 runway at London Fashion Week. Reminiscent of Mary-Kate Olsen’s fur-trimmed Balmain coat from the 2013 Met Gala, this particular stunner, along with the designer’s other iterations, seems to be what every It girl is wearing.

Recent findings suggest that the coat—crafted with silk tapestries dating back to the Qing dynasty and with hand-embroidered depictions of red-crowned cranes, bamboo leaves, and flowers—was undoubtedly the first wave in what would become a tsunami of a trend: opera coats. And while plenty of faux fur-trimmed coats have made their way onto the market, those featuring Chinese imagery like that on Ives’s iterations have taken center stage.

“There’s been a real change in how people perceive Chinese design,” Cheryl Leung, founder and creative director of Sau Lee, tells ELLE. Leung attributes the opera coat’s rise in popularity to fashion’s shift away from minimalism and consumers’ growing appetite for expressive pieces, richer fabrics, and textures. “Brocade is a great example because it has so much character,” she states. “The fabrics can be quite ornate, but when you put them into a modern silhouette or style them with something very simple, they feel completely different.”.

Chinese design has often been presented through a Western lens, but designers like Leung and Kim Shui are creating work rooted in their own cultural perspectives. Shui, the Chinese-American, Newly introduced York-based creative director behind her eponymous label, has long been drawn to Chinese garments and the ways they communicate identity. “I’m particularly interested in the visual language and craftsmanship of traditional Chinese garments, whether it’s the silhouette of the qipao (a traditional Chinese dress dating back to the Qing dynasty), the richness of brocade, or traditional techniques like embroidery and intricate knot closures,” Shui tells ELLE. “I look at these elements not as things to reproduce literally, but as a vocabulary that I can reinterpret.”.

Sources indicate that while the trend has gained widespread popularity, the Chinese design details behind it can sometimes be overlooked. “I’ve seen so many ‘trending winter coat’ videos featuring Chinese brocade coats with fur trim and traditional Chinese embroidered silk coats, but they don’t make any reference to their Chinese origins,” Shui says. “Instead of using terms like ‘qipao’ or ‘mandarin collar,’ creators will often describe these details generically as a ‘stand collar’ or ‘high neckline.’ It’s vital to acknowledge where these design elements come from and the history behind them—why erase the cultural context?”.

Leung sees the coat’s popularity as an opportunity to bring attention to its history and the designers reinterpreting it. Shui and her team have also been creating content about the histories of brocade, embroidery, and the qipao, as well as the cultural references behind her collections to bring more awareness of the craft to her audience.

In a recent development, “I do think there’s a difference between appreciating a design tradition and overlooking where it came from,” Leung states. “If a designer has been inspired by Chinese textiles, craftsmanship, or traditional clothing, acknowledging that doesn’t take anything away from their creativity. If anything, it gives the work more depth and helps people appreciate the original references.” Shui adds that brands outside the culture have a “responsibility to acknowledge their origins rather than presenting them as an entirely new aesthetic.”.

Fashion has been both a vehicle for cultural exchange and a product of it—and trends will undoubtedly come and go. Not everyone will be interested in the cultural history of the piece they buy—and Leung doesn’t necessarily think they need to be. Shui is happy to see people from all backgrounds embrace garments from outside of their own cultures. “I hope this renewed interest encourages people to look beyond the garment itself and discover the rich traditions and craftsmanship behind it,” she claims.

Industry News: The 7 Lessons I Learned About Skin After Losing 85 Pounds

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1433 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Harpersbazaar

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I lost 85 pounds without bariatric surgery.
  • Industry observers note that because I’m losing weight more slowly, I haven’t yet encountered loose skin, though I still have at least 50 more pounds to go.
  • Industry observers note that it’s a pretty unsexy topic—which is why it’s rarely, if ever, discussed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I lost 85 pounds without bariatric surgery. Weight loss has been on my mind basically my entire life, especially since I started this journey in earnest in July 2019. And, as proud of myself as I most certainly am for losing this weight and finally getting healthier, it is met toe-to-toe with pervasive anxiety and a nagging question: What about excess skin?

Industry observers note that because I’m losing weight more slowly, I haven’t yet encountered loose skin, though I still have at least 50 more pounds to go. I worry, perhaps too much, about whether I’ll make it to my goal weight without needing skin tightening at the end of this journey.

Industry observers note that it’s a pretty unsexy topic—which is why it’s rarely, if ever, discussed. But for those like me who are on major weight-loss journeys, or whose bodies have changed significantly through pregnancy, it’s a question that plagues us: Am I going to encounter excess skin the more weight I lose? And if I do, what can I do about it?

Industry observers note that apparently, I’m not the only one with questions, according to New York City plastic surgeon Lara Devgan. “Skin tightening remains one of the elusive black boxes in the world of plastic surgery,” she claims. That said, we’re all still learning about best practices—from me to medical professionals.

Industry observers note that so I decided to dig deeper. I rounded up five renowned dermatologists and plastic surgeons from across the country and asked them my questions. And here’s what they have to say.

Recent findings suggest that “Losing weight gradually rather than rapidly may prevent excess skin after major weight loss,” says Los Angeles–based dermatologist Harold Lancer. “However, rapid large-scale weight loss will invariably result in excess skin.” Devgan seconds that. “The best way to prevent skin laxity after weight loss is to do your best to lose weight at a slow and steady pace,” she says. “Although it may sound appealing to get to the finish line rapidly, that is actually the worst thing you can do in terms of skin laxity.” Losing weight slowly, she says, allows the skin to contract and shrink as the body shape changes.

Recent findings suggest that though I personally haven’t opted for weight loss surgery, many do—and there is zero shame in that. But because weight is lost more rapidly after surgery, the likelihood of excess skin increases, so experts recommend pairing weight loss surgery with a skin removal procedure. Why worry about excess skin, especially after faster weight loss? It’s “because collagen and elastin fibers are destroyed when skin is stretched significantly and remains stretched for an extended amount of time,” notes Upcoming York City plastic surgeon David Shafer. “Patients should blueprint on staged procedures if having a weight loss surgery followed by a skin removal surgery.”.

“Typically, younger patients with thicker and more sebaceous skin will have more skin contraction during weight loss due to better elasticity,” Devgan says. “Starting in the 20s, tissue elasticity begins to decline. Even in the absence of weight fluctuation, loss of tissue turgor and decreased firmness can be seen in midface descent in the late 20s, breast laxity in the 30s, abdominal laxity in the 40s, and extremity laxity in the 50s.”.

However, Devgan indicates everyone’s body is different. “There is a tremendous amount of variability in the human experience, so some patients may lose 50 pounds with minimal change in their body, while others can lose as few as 10 and see tissue laxity.” If you are genetically blessed with unusually superb tissue elasticity, Devgan says, it can be less dramatic. (And lucky you.).

Lifestyle choices can also factor in, Boston-based dermatologist Ranella Hirsch says. How long were you at the weight you started losing from? Are you a smoker? Do you spend a lot of time in the sun without protection? All these factors play into skin elasticity.

It has been revealed that “Using an emollient moisturizer rich in vitamin E will help improve the barrier protection of the skin and lock in moisture,” Devgan says. She also says the topical medical-grade ingredients you use on your face for firmness and tightness—like hyaluronic acid, peptides, niacin, squalene, vitamins C and B, retinol, and bakuchiol—can work elsewhere, too. “Most people focus on using these for the face and neck in their daily routines, but from a molecular perspective, their efficacy is present anywhere on the body.” But save your money on creams that promise you the world. “Losing large amounts of weight rapidly tends to leave skin behind,” Hirsch says. “Though creams with incredible claims abound, they actually do little.”.

Nécessaire The Body Lotion with Niacinamide.

Biossance Squalane + Caffeine Toning Body Cream.

Sol de Janeiro Bom Dia Bright Body Cream with Vitamin C.

Augustinus Bader The Body Cream.

U Beauty The SCULPT Arm Compound Body Serum.

Building muscle through weight training might help reduce the appearance of lax skin, New York City dermatologist Dendy Engelman claims. “This helps reduce the appearance by replacing the lost fat with muscle mass.”.

Recent findings suggest that nonsurgical options can help with loose skin after weight loss, but they won’t help with skin folds or hanging skin. “Noninvasive treatments such as laser and radiofrequency can help tighten the skin, but there is a limit to how much they can do,” Shafer adds. “Hanging skin generally needs to be surgically excised with procedures such as abdominoplasty, body lift, and arm lift.” Shafer states there’s a difference between loose skin and hanging skin. “It’s possible patients can manage and treat excess skin cases without undergoing skin removal surgery, such as if the skin is loose but not hanging.” He adds, “In that case, noninvasive treatments may be useful, but hanging skin most often requires surgical excision.”.

Sources indicate that “After major weight loss, people may have skin that hangs off their body,” Engelman says. “These heavy folds can cause health problems such as pain, inflammation, and frequent infections from the skin constantly rubbing together. This can happen during exercise or everyday activities. When a person is having functional issues because of their excess skin, it should be a sign that this problem needs to be addressed.” And, of course, everyone’s journey is different.

Lancer notes some individuals will tolerate moderate laxity and be happy with the weight-loss accomplishment; others will seek skin tightening for as little as a five-pound weight loss. But, he says, if plastic surgery does become the option on the table, “I would recommend getting at least three opinions from doctors who exclusively do excess body skin reduction. Once you select a doctor, do one small area on your body, so you can evaluate the procedure, how your body heals, and your results. Afterward, you can determine whether you’d like to proceed with a full-blown larger procedure.”.

He suggests consulting a dermatologist for nonsurgical options, then asking that doctor to recommend plastic surgeons who specialize in excess body skin reduction if you feel that is the right path for you. This is a major decision and shouldn’t be taken lightly. Bring medical professionals along for the entire weight-loss journey (even if you’ve already started) and ask all the questions: Which specific procedure is best? How much will it cost? Will insurance cover it? (From my research so far, no, if it is cosmetic, but perhaps yes if it would help correct something that limits your daily functionality.) No question is off-limits, and don’t try to make these decisions alone.

If this piece applies to you at all, whether it’s longstanding weight you carried, weight you lost during pregnancy, or somewhere in between, that means one thing: You’ve taken major steps toward better physical health, and that should be applauded. “Everyone’s weight loss story is different, and some days are harder than others,” Engelman indicates. “I say, try to be kind to yourself. You’ve just reached a huge accomplishment and should be proud of that.”.

In a recent development, devgan agrees. “Accomplishing a personal health goal like major weight loss is an incredible achievement that anyone should be proud of,” she states. “While excess skin can feel like a burden or source of self-consciousness, it is also a reminder of the metaphorical and literal shedding of the weight of a prior version of oneself. You cannot have a couture gown without a seam, and you cannot have a surgery without a scar. Life has limitations, but that does not make it less beautiful. It makes it more real.”.

Editor’s Note: This article originally ran in 2022.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, say you wanted to create the perfect pair of vintage-style military boots. First, you’d need a designer with impeccable taste and encyclopedic knowledge of vintage workwear; then you'd need a bootmaker with the requisite skills to produce it at the highest level. If everything went right, the result would be something like the Modèle 1917, a latest collaboration between famed Parisian creative director Gauthier Borsarello and renowned Canadian bootmaker Viberg.

In basic terms, the Modèle 1917 is a pair of boots based on the French Army’s 1917 “brodequin,” a design used by soldiers in the trenches of WWI, available in soft brown suede (Mud) and glossy textured black leather (Pavement). But there’s nothing basic about them. The design comes courtesy of Borsarello, a top-tier collector of vintage workwear and the creative mind behind Gersaint Paris and L’Etiquette magazine. Viberg, a third-generation, family-owned boot specialist, got its start making footwear for forestry crews in British Columbia, and it still builds every pair in its Vancouver Island workshop. While it doesn’t make boots for smokejumpers and loggers anymore, old-school shoemaking techniques like a channeled insole Goodyear welt and stitchdown construction ensure their footwear retains its heirloom-level durability.

Industry observers note that the backstory of the “brodequin” begins with the Mdl. 1893, a hobnail-soled marching boot created for French infantrymen in the late 1800s that remained in use until the 1950s. In the First World War, the brodequin’s iron-studded soles and sturdy uppers proved ideally suited to the muddy conditions of the trenches, and American troops soon adopted them in place of their inferior M1904 Marching Shoes. “To me, it’s the blueprint for many combat boots across different countries after WWI,” says Borsarello. “I love the idea that France inspired others after fighting side by side in the trenches. They’re very simple, yet instantly recognizable at the same time.”.

For all of its strengths in the field, the original brodequin—whose nickname pays tongue-in-cheek homage to a medieval torture device—wasn’t what you’d call a comfortable boot, especially by modern standards. “They were so stiff that they were almost impossible to walk in,” Borsarello admits. This created something of a design challenge.

Industry observers note that to stay as true as possible to the original, Borsarello and Viberg designed the boots on a period-correct “pied haricot” (bean-shaped) last, with a cotton twill lining, solid brass hardware, and reinforced panels that support the midfoot so the forefoot can move freely. To make the Modèle M1917 something you’d actually want to wear, they replaced the hobnailed soles with rubber ones and swapped the original roughout leather for supple American-tanned Horween. The result is a pair of boots that are as comfortable as they are durable, not to mention surprisingly versatile. In other words, exactly what you’d expect from a meeting of these formidable talents.

With a fridge full of Thanksgiving leftovers, the possibilities are endless. But leftovers reach their most perfect form in a sandwich, where all the components play off one other for a few transcendent bites.

These Thanksgiving sandwiches make the most of what you’ve got, whether that’s a few slices of turkey or enough stuffing and cranberry sauce for an encore. Go all in with a gooey melt, load a pita with spiced turkey and crunchy vegetables, or give turkey the chicken salad treatment. There’s no need for post-holiday blues when a leftover turkey sandwich is on the horizon.

Industry observers note that this turkey sandwich takes inspiration from one of the all-time greats: the tuna melt. You might be surprised by how well turkey takes to the format. For the full diner experience, serve it with potato chips and a dill pickle.

Recent findings suggest that though the recipe calls for cooked chicken, you guessed it—you can swap in leftover turkey seamlessly. The apple and fennel both provide lots of crunch and freshness.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that christmas might get the lights, presents, and monthlong buildup, but Ina Garten has a few thoughts about which holiday really deserves the fuss. And if a certain Thanksgiving side dish comes up in conversation, the Barefoot Contessa’s face might tell you everything you need to know.

It has been revealed that during the November 18 episode of her Happy Hour with Ina Garten podcast, the cookbook author asked guest Rose Byrne about her first Thanksgiving in the United States. The Australian actress recalled attending a Friendsgiving, with everyone contributing something to the meal, and Garten immediately wanted to know whether the whole thing had been organized in advance or “if everyone just showed up with string beans.”.

Things got even funnier when Byrne mentioned candied yams topped with marshmallows, something she found “pretty weird.” Garten visibly grimaced at the mention of the dish, chuckling before describing them as “very American." Judging by that expression alone, I wouldn't expect to find the dish making an appearance at her next dinner party.

Garten's feelings about Thanksgiving itself, however, are considerably warmer, especially when compared to Christmas.

"Thanksgiving is just quiet. It's all that one day and it's all about the food," she explained, pointing out that Christmas comes with gifts, parties, and a whole lot more going on.

In a recent development, it makes sense coming from someone who’s built an entire career around bringing people together over a good meal. And we already know Garten’s enthusiasm for Thanksgiving extends beyond what’s on the plate. Last year, she shared her favorite wines to serve with Thanksgiving dinner, including Morgon, a lighter French red from the Beaujolais region, and white Burgundies like Meursault or Montrachet to accompany the turkey. She also likes a Sonoma Valley Pinot Noir, giving the American holiday a little hometown representation in the wine department.

At least now I know that if I ever get invited to Thanksgiving at Ina’s, I'll gladly let her handle the wine—and I know to keep the marshmallow-topped yams at home.

The 7 Most Common Mistakes Home Cooks Make When Cooking Mashed Potatoes

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (620 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a traditional Thanksgiving meal, mashed potatoes are a seemingly simple side dish that does a lot of heavy lifting.
  • Recent findings suggest that mashed potatoes prove you can transform even the humblest ingredients into something magical.
  • Thankfully, those mistakes are 100% avoidable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a traditional Thanksgiving meal, mashed potatoes are a seemingly simple side dish that does a lot of heavy lifting. They're the perfect vessel for a puddle of gravy, and they’re a creamy complement to everything else on your plate—yes, even your aunt's questionable green bean casserole.

Recent findings suggest that mashed potatoes prove you can transform even the humblest ingredients into something magical. And yet, we've all somehow still eaten bad ones. With a recipe this basic, even the smallest mistakes have nowhere to hide.

Thankfully, those mistakes are 100% avoidable. We rounded up the most common ways to mess up mashed potatoes so that yours turn out as delicious as possible this holiday season.

Recent findings suggest that it doesn’t matter if you cut your potatoes into a fine dice or rough chunks. Whatever size you pick, stick with it. Making sure your potato pieces are roughly the same size will help them all cook at the same rate. If your knife work is haphazard, you may end up with some pieces that are perfectly cooked, others that are waterlogged and mushy, and some that are still firm in the center.

Like pasta, potatoes need a good amount of seasoning to really shine—which is why salting the cooking water is so vital. You can be generous with the salt, since much of it stays in the water and ends up going down the drain. When you start seasoning early in the cooking process, it’s easier to build flavor and adjust as you go.

According to recent reports, in the hustle of cooking all of your Thanksgiving dishes, you may be tempted to boil your potatoes ahead of time and mash them later in the day. But it’s always better to work with potatoes while they’re still hot and easier to mash. Waiting until they’re cool will likely require far more elbow grease—and you’ll still end up with uneven chunks.

Sources indicate that A smooth, creamy mash is the height of decadence. To make sure the potatoes are lump-free, some people may reach for a blender—but this is one of the most consequential mistakes you can make. Potatoes are naturally starchy, and the more you work them, the more starch gets released from their cell walls. Breaking out the blender may be well-intentioned, but it can leave you with potatoes that are gummy and gluey. Instead, opt for the right tool, like a hand masher, food mill, or potato ricer.

Recent findings suggest that another important thing to consider is that potato starches continue absorbing moisture as mashed potatoes sit. They can soak up the milk you’ve added, leaving your potatoes dry and dense. Don’t be afraid to add more liquid—or at least keep some extra on hand to loosen up your mash before serving.

In a recent development, anthony Bourdain famously pointed to generous amounts of salt and butter as part of what makes restaurant food taste so good. That’s especially true for mashed potatoes. You may be scared to add more than a light sprinkle of salt, but don’t forget to taste and adjust the seasoning before serving. A little extra salt can make all the difference for your Thanksgiving dinner.

Recent findings suggest that whether you’re feeding your immediate family or a small army, you should always make a big batch of mashed potatoes. This side is one of the most popular components of a Thanksgiving menu, so it never hurts to make extra. It’s also one of the most versatile dishes for repurposing leftovers. You can transform them into gnocchi, shepherd’s pie, or crispy fried croquettes. It may require more mashing in the moment, but your future self will thank you.
